tagline: Every cell is only as healthy as the blood that reaches it — follow the flow.
overview: Perfusion is the flow of blood through arteries and capillaries delivering oxygen and nutrients to cells and removing wastes. It depends on a working pump (the heart), open vessels, adequate blood volume, and balanced clotting. Nurses protect perfusion by assessing heart sounds, pulses, and blood pressure accurately, understanding the diagnostic tests used, recognizing the alterations in the B.E. case study (stroke, fluid overload/pulmonary edema, hypertensive crisis), and promoting heart-healthy lifestyles across the lifespan.

topics.title: Cardiac Anatomy & Circulation
topics.summary: A four-chambered pump in a protective sac drives two circuits in series — pulmonary and systemic — while the coronary arteries feed the pump itself.

sections.heading: Location and pericardium
sections.body: The heart is a hollow, cone-shaped organ weighing less than 1 lb, located in the mediastinum of the thoracic cavity between the sternum and vertebral column and flanked laterally by the lungs. Its apex points down and to the left, near the 5th intercostal space (ICS) at the left midclavicular line.
bullets: Pericardium — a double layer of fibroserous membrane that encases the heart, anchors it to surrounding structures (the pericardial sac), and fits snugly to keep the heart from overfilling.
Parietal layer (outer) and visceral layer (inner); the space between them is the pericardial cavity.
Serous fluid in the cavity cushions the heart as it contracts. If excess fluid collects and compresses the heart, it can be removed by pericardiocentesis (see Diagnostic Tests).

sections.heading: Layers of the heart wall
bullets: Epicardium — outermost layer; covers the entire heart and great vessels and folds over to form the parietal layer of the pericardium.
Myocardium — middle layer of specialized cardiac muscle cells (myofibrils) that provides the bulk of the contractile muscle.
Endocardium — innermost thin membrane; its innermost layer is smooth endothelial cells lining the chambers and valves.

sections.heading: Chambers and valves
sections.body: Four hollow chambers: right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), left atrium (LA), and left ventricle (LV). Valves between chambers allow one-way (unidirectional) flow.
bullets: Atrioventricular (AV) valves separate atria from ventricles — tricuspid (right) and mitral (left). Closure produces S1.
Semilunar valves connect ventricles to the great vessels — pulmonic (RV → pulmonary artery) and aortic (LV → aorta). Closure produces S2.

sections.heading: Blood flow sequence
sections.body: Superior/inferior venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery (carries deoxygenated blood) → pulmonary capillaries (gas exchange) → pulmonary veins (oxygenated) → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → systemic arteries → capillaries → systemic veins → venae cavae.

sections.heading: Three circulations
bullets: Pulmonary — right side of the heart, pulmonary artery, pulmonary capillaries, pulmonary vein.
Systemic — moves blood to the periphery: left side of the heart, aorta and its branches, systemic arteries, capillaries supplying the brain and peripheral tissues, systemic veins, and venae cavae.

Coronary — the vessels that supply the heart muscle itself. The left coronary artery branches into the anterior descending and circumflex arteries; the right coronary artery gives rise to the posterior descending artery. Coronary arteries fill mainly during diastole.

table.caption: The three circulations
rows: Right heart → pulmonary artery → pulmonary capillaries → pulmonary vein
Picks up oxygen and unloads CO₂ in the lungs
Left heart → aorta → arteries → capillaries → veins → venae cavae
Delivers oxygenated blood to the brain and peripheral tissues
Left coronary (anterior descending, circumflex); right coronary (posterior descending)

pearls: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood — a favorite trick question.
Tachycardia shortens diastole — and diastole is when the coronaries fill. A fast heart is a hungry, underfed heart.
Right heart problems back up into the body (venae cavae → JVD, edema); left heart problems back up into the lungs (crackles, dyspnea).
redFlags: Chest pain means the coronary circulation may not be meeting the myocardium's oxygen demand — assess with PQRST, obtain an ECG as ordered, and notify the provider.

topics.title: Heart Sounds & Cardiac Auscultation
topics.summary: Valve closure makes the "lub-dub"; extra sounds and murmurs tell you about ventricular filling, stiffness, and disrupted flow.

sections.heading: Normal sounds
bullets: S1 ("lub") — closure of the AV valves (mitral, tricuspid) at the start of systole (ventricular contraction); loudest at the apex; coincides with the carotid pulse.
S2 ("dub") — closure of the semilunar valves (aortic, pulmonic) at the start of diastole (ventricular relaxation); loudest at the base.
Physiologic split S2 — normal when caused by the increase in intrathoracic pressure during inspiration; best heard at the pulmonic area.

sections.heading: Extra sounds (gallops)
bullets: S3 (ventricular gallop) — early diastole, just after S2 ("Ken-TUC-ky"); rapid filling of the ventricle. Can be normal in children, young adults, and women in the third trimester of pregnancy; in other adults, especially with heart failure, it suggests fluid (volume) overload.
S4 (atrial gallop) — late diastole, just before S1 ("TEN-nes-see"); the atrium contracting into a stiff ventricle. Can be heard in children, well-conditioned athletes, and healthy older adults.
S3 and S4 are low-pitched — listen with the bell at the apex.

sections.heading: Murmurs
sections.body: A murmur is a swishing or blowing sound caused by disruption of blood flow into the heart, between chambers, or from the heart into the pulmonary or aortic system. Newborns may have nonpathologic (innocent) murmurs; in a healthy adult the expected finding is "no murmurs on auscultation."

sections.heading: Auscultation sequence
sections.body: After inspecting, palpating the precordium and carotids, and percussing, auscultate the heart at five areas: aortic → pulmonic → Erb's point → tricuspid → mitral ("APE To Man"), then the carotid and apical pulses. Use the diaphragm for higher-pitched S1/S2 and the bell (light pressure) for low-pitched S3, S4, and murmurs. Expected: equal, audible S1 and S2 heard at Erb's point (3rd ICS, left sternal border) and no murmurs.

pearls: S3 = "sloshing in" (volume); S4 = "stiff wall." A new S3 in an adult with heart failure → check lungs, weight trend, and I&O.
Palpate the carotid pulse while listening — the sound that coincides with the pulse is S1.
An S3 in a 35-week pregnant client with normal vital signs is an expected finding to document, not an emergency.
redFlags: New S3 with crackles, dyspnea, edema, and rising weight in an adult → fluid overload/worsening heart failure.

topics.title: Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload & Contractility
topics.summary: CO = HR × SV; stroke volume rises or falls with preload, afterload, and contractility.

sections.heading: Key definitions
bullets: Cardiac cycle — one heartbeat: systole (ventricular contraction) + diastole (relaxation and filling).
Stroke volume (SV) — volume ejected by the ventricle with each beat (about 60–100 mL; average ~70 mL).
Cardiac output (CO) = HR × SV; normal about 4–8 L/min (e.g., 72 × 70 mL ≈ 5 L/min).
Ejection fraction (EF) — the percentage of the blood in the ventricle that is ejected with each beat; normal about 50–70%.

sections.heading: Heart rate
sections.body: Heart rate is affected by direct and indirect autonomic nervous system (ANS) stimulation: the SNS increases heart rate, and parasympathetic vagal tone slows it. Reflex regulation occurs in response to systemic BP through activation of sensory receptors (baroreceptors). Extremes reduce CO: bradycardia lowers output directly, and very fast rates shorten diastolic filling time so stroke volume falls.

sections.heading: Determinants of stroke volume
bullets: Contractility — the capability of cardiac muscle fibers to shorten. Poor contractility reduces blood flow from the heart, increases ventricular pressures, and reduces CO.

Preload — the amount of cardiac muscle fiber tension (stretch) at the end of diastole; influenced by venous return and ventricular compliance. Continuous overstretching (increased preload, e.g., fluid overload) → ineffective contraction. Preload falls with bleeding or dehydration.

Afterload — the force the ventricles must overcome to eject blood; affected by vascular tone. As workload rises, myocardial O₂ consumption rises; if the heart cannot meet the demand, a vicious cycle begins. Very low afterload (marked vasodilation) decreases blood flow into the circulation.

sections.heading: Clinical indicators of CO
sections.body: At the bedside, CO is judged by end-organ perfusion: level of consciousness, skin color and temperature, peripheral pulses, urine output (about 30 mL/hr or more in adults), and BP compared with baseline. Critically ill clients may have invasive hemodynamic monitoring catheters.

table.caption: What changes the determinants
rows: SNS stimulation, fever, pain, anxiety, exercise
Bleeding, dehydration, diuretics, supine vena cava compression in late pregnancy

pearls: Pre-load = the "pre"-filling stretch; after-load = the pressure the ventricle pushes against "after" the valve opens.
A drop in urine output is often the earliest objective sign that cardiac output is falling.
A faster heart rate raises CO only up to a point — very fast rates cut filling time and CO falls.
redFlags: Urine output <30 mL/hr, new confusion, or cool, clammy skin → signs of low cardiac output; report promptly.

topics.title: Conduction System & Action Potential
topics.summary: The heart fires itself: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers.

sections.heading: Pathway
sections.body: Self-excitation lets cardiac muscle cells initiate and transmit impulses without an outside stimulus.
bullets: SA node — the pacemaker (normally 60–100/min).
Impulse travels across the atria to the AV node, where it is slowed so the ventricles can fill (backup rate about 40–60/min).

Then through the bundle of His at the AV junction, down the interventricular septum through the right and left bundle branches, and out to the Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls (backup rate about 20–40/min).

sections.heading: Action potential
sections.body: Movement of sodium, potassium, and calcium ions creates the electrical impulse that stimulates contraction and produces the waveforms recorded by the ECG. At rest the cell is polarized — negative inside, positive outside.
bullets: Depolarization — the cell becomes more positive, reaches threshold potential, and fires an action potential that spreads to surrounding cells → contraction.
Repolarization — the cell regains its negative charge and returns to the resting, polarized state.

Refractory period protects cardiac muscle from spasm and tetany: absolute — no depolarization regardless of stimulus; relative — a greater-than-normal stimulus is needed; supernormal — even a mild stimulus causes depolarization.
Many dysrhythmias are triggered during the refractory and supernormal periods.

sections.heading: ECG correlation
bullets: P wave — atrial depolarization.
PR interval (0.12–0.20 s) — time for the impulse to pass through the AV node.
QRS (<0.12 s) — ventricular depolarization.
T wave — ventricular repolarization.

sections.heading: Pulse vs. heartbeat
sections.body: The pulse is the wave of blood created by LV contraction and represents stroke volume output. In a healthy person the pulse reflects every heartbeat. With an irregular rhythm such as atrial fibrillation, some beats have too little filling time to produce a peripheral pulse — the basis of a pulse deficit. Factors affecting the pulse include medications, activity, position, fever, pain, and anxiety.

pearls: Electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium) drive the action potential — imbalances often show up on the monitor as dysrhythmias.
Fibrosis of the AV node with aging can cause AV block; a new slow pulse with dizziness in an older adult needs an ECG.
Atrial fibrillation (in B.E.'s history) lets clots form in the atria and is a leading cause of embolic stroke.
redFlags: New slow or irregular pulse with dizziness, hypotension, or altered mental status → notify the provider and obtain an ECG as ordered.

topics.title: Blood Pressure: Determinants & Accurate Measurement
topics.summary: BP reflects the pump, the resistance of the vessels, and the volume and viscosity of blood — and a wrong cuff or a rushed technique can misclassify a client.

sections.heading: Terms
bullets: Arterial pressure — the pressure of blood flowing through the arteries.
Systolic BP — pressure from contraction of the ventricles.
Diastolic BP — pressure when the ventricles are at rest.
Pulse pressure — the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure (e.g., 120 − 80 = 40 mm Hg).
Typical healthy adult BP is 120/80 mm Hg, but it varies considerably — the nurse must know the client's baseline.

sections.heading: Determinants of BP
bullets: Pumping action of the heart (cardiac output).
Peripheral vascular resistance — increased by decreased capacity of arterioles and capillaries, loss of arterial compliance (aging, atherosclerosis), and increased blood viscosity.
Blood volume — decreased by bleeding or dehydration; increased by fluid retention.
Blood viscosity — thicker blood (e.g., more red cells) raises resistance.
Other factors: age, stress and pain, race, sex, time of day, medications, activity, weight, and smoking.

sections.heading: Correct technique (indirect, auscultatory)
bullets: Client rests quietly about 5 minutes, back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed; no talking.
Bare upper arm; arm supported at heart level.
Correct cuff size — a cuff that is too small or narrow gives a falsely HIGH reading; too large gives a falsely low reading.

Palpatory estimate first: inflate until the radial/brachial pulse disappears, then inflate about 30 mm Hg above that point for the auscultated reading — this prevents missing an auscultatory gap. Palpation is also used when Korotkoff sounds cannot be heard and amplifying equipment is not available.
Deflate slowly (about 2–3 mm Hg per second); wait 1–2 minutes before repeating on the same arm.
Common errors: haste and subconscious bias (the nurse "hears" the value expected).

sections.heading: Methods and Korotkoff sounds
sections.body: Direct measurement uses a catheter in the brachial, radial, or femoral artery. Indirect (noninvasive) methods are auscultatory (Korotkoff sounds) and palpatory.
bullets: Phase I — first clear tapping = systolic.
Phases II–III — swishing, then crisp tapping.
Phase IV — muffling; recorded as diastolic in children.
Phase V — silence = diastolic in adults.

Auscultatory gap — temporary disappearance of sounds over the brachial artery when cuff pressure is high (common with hypertension and stiff arteries); without a palpated estimate the nurse may record a falsely low systolic.

sections.heading: Sites and limbs to avoid
sections.body: Standard site is the upper arm (brachial artery) with a standard stethoscope; the thigh is the alternative. Do not measure BP on a limb with:
bullets: Injury or disease of the shoulder, arm, or hand (or hip, knee, ankle)
A cast or bulky bandage on any part of the limb
Surgical removal of axillary (or hip) lymph nodes on that side
An IV infusion in that limb
An arteriovenous fistula in that limb

sections.heading: Hypotension and orthostatic hypotension
sections.body: Hypotension is a below-normal BP reading. Orthostatic (postural) hypotension usually results from peripheral vasodilation; causes include dehydration, bleeding, severe burns, and certain analgesics (and other medications such as antihypertensives and diuretics). Assess by placing the client supine first, then assisting to sit or stand, and measuring BP and pulse in each position; a drop of about 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing is significant. Stay with the client and return them to bed if they become symptomatic.

table.caption: Common measurement errors
rows: Back or arm unsupported, legs crossed, talking
Repeating too soon on the same arm

pearls: Always interpret BP against the client's baseline — 100/60 may be normal for one client and a warning sign for another.
When a BP is unexpectedly high, first recheck with correct technique and cuff size before acting on it.
Orthostatic vital signs: the nurse stays at the bedside — the client may faint on standing.
redFlags: BP above about 180/120 with headache, confusion, chest pain, dyspnea, or visual change → possible hypertensive emergency; notify the provider immediately.
Hypotension with altered mental status or low urine output → inadequate perfusion.

topics.title: Pulse, Peripheral & Cardiovascular Assessment
topics.summary: A focused history, a systematic inspection–palpation–percussion–auscultation exam, and accurate pulses reveal how well blood is reaching the tissues.

sections.heading: Health history (careful questioning)
bullets: Symptoms: pain, fatigue, shortness of breath, lightheadedness.
Chest pain using PQRST — Provoking/Palliating factors, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity, Timing.
Current and past medical history, lifestyle (smoking, diet, exercise, alcohol), and stress and coping.
Observation during the interview: dyspnea, edema, cyanosis and pallor, mental status, and jugular vein distention (JVD).

sections.heading: Physical exam — order and normal findings
sections.body: Use inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation, correlating findings with landmarks (sternum, clavicles, ribs). Sequence: inspect head and neck (eyes, ears, lips, face, skull, neck vessels — note symmetry) → inspect upper extremities, chest, abdomen, lower extremities → palpate precordium and carotid pulses → percuss for cardiac borders → auscultate the heart (aortic, pulmonic, Erb's point, tricuspid, mitral) and the carotid and apical pulses.
bullets: Skin color even; lips smooth without cyanosis; eyes symmetric; earlobes flat without creases.
Jugular veins flat, not visible (client upright/at 45°).
Carotid pulses palpated (one side at a time) and auscultated bilaterally; symmetric.
Fingernails slightly curved or flat, no cyanosis; respirations regular, even, unlabored.
No pulsations over the precordium (aortic pulsation may be visible in the suprasternal notch in thin clients); slight vibration palpable at the apex.
Dull percussion over the heart up to the midclavicular line at the 5th ICS.
Lower extremities: even temperature and color, symmetric hair distribution.

sections.heading: Pulse sites and characteristics
sections.body: Sites: temporal, carotid, apical, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, pedal (dorsalis pedis). Assess rate, rhythm, volume (amplitude), arterial wall elasticity, and bilateral equality by palpation or auscultation; use a Doppler ultrasound stethoscope for difficult-to-assess pulses. The pulse is affected by medication, physical activity, and position — know the client's baseline.
bullets: Count a full 60 seconds when the rhythm is irregular or at the apex.

sections.heading: Apical pulse and apical-radial pulse
sections.body: Take an apical pulse (5th ICS, left midclavicular line) when the peripheral pulse is irregular or unavailable, in clients with known cardiovascular, pulmonary, or renal disease, in newborns, infants, and children up to 2–3 years, and before giving medications that affect heart rate. For an apical-radial pulse, two nurses count simultaneously for 60 seconds using one watch. The rates are normally identical; apical > radial indicates a problem. Pulse deficit = any difference between the two rates. The radial rate is never greater than the apical rate.

sections.heading: Jugular vein distention
sections.body: With the head of the bed at 30–45°, jugular veins are normally flat. Visible distention (or pulsation more than about 3–4 cm above the sternal angle) reflects elevated right-sided pressure — seen with right-sided heart failure and fluid overload.

table.caption: Pulse volume (amplitude) grading
rows: Confirm with Doppler; report if new

pearls: Compare bilaterally — asymmetry matters more than any single number.
In an older adult with hand or arm tremors, the radial pulse can be hard to count; use the apical pulse.
Count the pulse before painful or upsetting procedures — pain and crying raise it, especially in children.
redFlags: A newly absent pulse with a cool, pale limb → notify the provider immediately.
Apical rate greater than radial rate (pulse deficit) → some beats are not perfusing the periphery; report and monitor.

topics.title: Hemostasis, Fibrinolysis & VTE Prevention
topics.summary: The body stops bleeding in steps — vasoconstriction, platelet plug, coagulation — then dissolves the clot through fibrinolysis; imbalance causes bleeding or clotting.

sections.heading: Steps of hemostasis
sections.body: Hemostasis is the process by which the body slows and stops the flow of blood; its regulation is essential to perfusion.
bullets: 1. Vasoconstriction — triggered by substances released at the injury site and by nerve impulses from pain receptors; reduces blood loss immediately.
2. Platelet plug formation — platelets stick together and close the hole in the vessel; this seal is temporary.
3. Coagulation cascade — clotting factors produce fibrin strands, forming a larger, stronger patch than the platelet plug.

sections.heading: Fibrinolysis
sections.body: Fibrinolysis is the breakdown of the clot. It begins when new, healthy tissue at the injury site secretes tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), which activates plasmin; plasmin digests the fibrin strands and dissolves the clot. Thrombolytic medications such as alteplase are manufactured tPA — they dissolve clots (e.g., in ischemic stroke), and their main risk is bleeding, including bleeding in the brain.

sections.heading: Medications and hemostasis (application)
bullets: Antiplatelet drugs (e.g., aspirin) interfere with the platelet plug → cuts bleed longer.
Anticoagulants interfere with the coagulation cascade → prevent new clots and clot growth but do not dissolve existing clots.
Thrombolytics (tPA) activate fibrinolysis → dissolve existing clots.

sections.heading: Venous stasis and compression devices
sections.body: Blood that pools (stasis) — from immobility, bed rest after surgery or stroke, or the enlarging uterus in pregnancy — increases the risk of venous thrombosis. Pregnancy also raises fibrinogen and clotting factors, adding to the risk. Nurses promote circulation and assess application of compression devices.
bullets: Sequential compression devices (SCDs) — measure the leg for the correct sleeve; about two fingers should fit between sleeve and leg; check that tubing is not kinked and the pump cycles; remove periodically per policy to inspect the skin and check pulses.
Compression stockings — measure for size; apply smoothly without wrinkles; never roll the top down (creates a tourniquet); remove daily for skin care.
Do not apply compression to a leg with signs of a clot (new unilateral swelling, warmth, tenderness) — hold the device and notify the provider.
Also: early ambulation, leg exercises (ankle pumps), and adequate fluids.

table.caption: Hemostasis at a glance
rows: Platelets stick together at the injury (temporary)
Fibrin strands form a stronger patch

pearls: Pregnancy increases fibrin, fibrinogen, and clotting factors VII, VIII, IX, and X, yet clotting time stays about the same — and venous thrombosis risk rises.
Never massage a painful, swollen calf; it can dislodge a clot.
The RN assesses the legs and decides whether compression is safe before SCDs or stockings are applied.
redFlags: New headache, neurologic change, or bleeding during thrombolytic (tPA) therapy → stop the infusion and notify the provider.
New unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and pain → possible venous clot; do not apply compression to that leg; notify the provider.

topics.title: Diagnostic Tests for Perfusion
topics.summary: Labs, ECG, imaging, stress testing, and catheterization determine cardiac function — and each carries nursing responsibilities.

sections.heading: Cardiac blood tests
bullets: Troponin — the most specific marker of heart muscle injury. It takes a few hours to rise after injury, so serial draws are required; one normal early value does not rule out injury.
CK-MB (MB isoenzyme) and creatine kinase (CK) — older markers of muscle injury; CK-MB is the heart-specific form.
Serum cholesterol, triglycerides, and lipids — screen for cardiovascular risk (see table).

sections.heading: ECG and imaging
bullets: ECG — records the heart's electrical activity: rhythm, rate, and signs of ischemia or injury.
Chest x-ray, CT, MRI, PET — heart size, lung congestion, structure, and blood flow. Electron beam CT identifies calcium blockages in the coronary arteries.
Echocardiogram — noninvasive ultrasound of wall motion, valves, and ejection fraction.
Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) — probe passed into the esophagus with sedation and throat anesthesia; NPO before; afterward keep NPO until the gag reflex returns and monitor for aspiration.

sections.heading: Stress testing
bullets: Exercise stress test — ECG and BP monitored as workload increases on a treadmill or bicycle; wear comfortable shoes; avoid caffeine and tobacco beforehand per instructions.

Chemical (pharmacologic) stress test — for clients who cannot exercise; a medication stresses the heart instead. Caffeine is usually held beforehand because it can block some stress agents — follow the prep instructions.
Often combined with a radionuclide (nuclear) test or stress echocardiography.
Stop the test and report chest pain, severe dyspnea, dizziness, dysrhythmias, or a drop in BP.

sections.heading: Cardiac catheterization with coronary angiography
sections.body: A catheter is threaded through an artery (femoral or radial) into the heart, and contrast dye outlines the coronary arteries (angiography/arteriography).
bullets: Before: informed consent; NPO per protocol; ask about allergy to contrast; check kidney function (creatinine) and bleeding risk (coagulation studies, anticoagulant use); mark distal pulses; tell the client a warm, flushing feeling may occur with the dye.

After femoral access: bed rest as ordered with the leg straight and HOB ≤30°; check the site, distal pulses, color, temperature, and sensation frequently; encourage fluids to flush the contrast; monitor urine output.
After radial access: check the site, radial pulse, and hand color and warmth; avoid BP and blood draws on that arm.
Bleeding: apply firm direct pressure just above the puncture site and call for help.

sections.heading: Pericardiocentesis
sections.body: Needle aspiration of fluid from the pericardial sac, used for diagnosis and to relieve fluid that is compressing the heart. The nurse monitors ECG, BP, and heart sounds during and after the procedure.

pearls: Troponin is the "go-to" heart-injury marker — trend it; never rule out injury on one early value.
After a femoral cath, a sudden "warm, wet" feeling at the groin = bleeding until proven otherwise.
Contrast is hard on the kidneys — watch creatinine and urine output after the procedure.
redFlags: Loss of distal pulse or a cool, pale, numb leg after catheterization → arterial compromise; notify the provider immediately.
Enlarging swelling at the puncture site, or hypotension with tachycardia after catheterization → bleeding; apply pressure and call for help.

topics.title: Stroke, Heart Failure, Pulmonary Edema & Hypertensive Crisis
topics.exemplar: Case Study: B.E. — Ischemic Stroke to Hypertensive Crisis
topics.summary: Alterations in perfusion cascade: in the B.E. case, an embolic stroke is followed by fluid overload, pulmonary edema, and a hypertensive emergency.

sections.heading: Alterations and prevalence
sections.body: An alteration in perfusion may be the primary diagnosis or secondary to another condition, and clients usually have alterations in other concepts too (oxygenation, acid-base balance, fluids and electrolytes, cognition, comfort, cellular regulation).
bullets: Respiratory acidosis — acute with acute ventilatory failure; chronic usually secondary to other conditions.
Metabolic acidosis — causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and increased pulmonary vascular pressures → right ventricular failure and myocardial depression.
High blood pressure affects about 29% of American adults; heart disease is the leading cause of death for men and women; heart failure is the primary cause of death for about 55,000 people each year.
Stroke affects about 795,000 Americans each year, causes about 130,000 deaths (1 in 20), and is the top cause of long-term disability.

sections.heading: Stroke recognition — BE-FAST
bullets: Balance — sudden loss of balance or coordination
Eyes — sudden vision loss or double vision
Face — facial droop
Arm — arm (or leg) weakness or numbness
Speech — slurred speech or difficulty forming words
Time — note the time last known well and activate the stroke alert/911 immediately

Motor pathways cross: a right-hemisphere stroke causes left-sided weakness, often with left-sided neglect and impulsivity; a left-hemisphere stroke causes right-sided weakness and, in most people, aphasia.

sections.heading: Acute ischemic stroke — nursing priorities
bullets: Airway, breathing, circulation; frequent neuro checks and vital signs; point-of-care glucose (low glucose can mimic stroke).
Emergency CT scan to distinguish an ischemic (clot) stroke from bleeding.
Clot-dissolving therapy (tPA) may be given for eligible clients — the nurse watches closely for bleeding and neuro changes.
NPO until a bedside swallow screen is passed — aspiration pneumonia is a major complication; keep HOB elevated and suction as needed.
Atrial fibrillation is a common source of clots that travel to the brain.

sections.heading: Heart failure — left vs. right
sections.body: Left-sided failure backs blood into the lungs: dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, cough, S3, fatigue, confusion, decreased urine output. Right-sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins: JVD, dependent pitting edema, weight gain, abdominal fullness. Left-sided failure is the most common cause of right-sided failure. Continuous overstretching of the ventricle (high preload) makes contraction less effective.

sections.heading: Acute pulmonary edema
sections.body: Fluid floods the alveoli when pressure in the left heart rises (fluid overload, worsening heart failure, severe hypertension). Signs: severe dyspnea, anxiety, tachypnea, crackles throughout, pink frothy sputum, falling SpO₂, diaphoresis.
bullets: Position upright (high Fowler's) to reduce venous return and ease breathing.
Oxygen; suction; prepare for ventilatory support if oxygenation fails.
Give diuretics and other medications as prescribed; strict intake and output, daily weights, and fluid restriction as ordered.

sections.heading: Hypertensive crisis
bullets: Severe hypertension — BP above about 180/120 without acute organ damage.

Hypertensive emergency — severe hypertension with acute target-organ damage: brain (severe headache, confusion, seizures, stroke), heart (chest pain), lungs (acute pulmonary edema), kidneys (rising creatinine, low urine output).
Report immediately. BP is lowered in the ICU in a controlled, gradual way per the provider — lowering it too quickly can reduce blood flow to the brain, heart, and kidneys.
Assess and treat contributing causes: pain, agitation, a full bladder, hypoxia, and missed home medications.

sections.heading: Unfolding case: B.E.
sections.body: Part 1: A 64-year-old man collapses at home after confusion, left-arm numbness and tingling, double vision, slurred speech, and left facial droop. History: CAD, hypertension, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, diabetes. T 37.2, P 91, RR 24, BP 182/98. After regaining consciousness he has left-sided weakness, slurred speech, and difficulty forming words. Part 2: CT confirms an ischemic stroke of the right parietal/temporal region. He cannot manage his secretions, work of breathing increases, and SpO₂ is in the high 80s on a nonrebreather. At 36 hours: bilateral crackles worse on the right, pitting edema, markedly decreased urine output, and he is difficult to arouse and oriented to person only — fluid overload/pulmonary edema with possible aspiration (the right mainstem bronchus is straighter). Part 3: Day 4, on a ventilator: BP 258/128, P 112, crackles throughout, pink frothy secretions, minimally responsive and grimacing during a sedation vacation — a hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary edema; pain may be contributing.

pearls: Time is brain: the most important fact to obtain in suspected stroke is when the client was last known well.
Left = Lungs; Right = Rest of the body.
Low urine output with crackles and edema means poor cardiac output with fluid overload — not dehydration.
redFlags: Any sudden BE-FAST finding → activate the stroke alert and keep the client NPO.
Pink frothy sputum, falling SpO₂ despite oxygen, and crackles throughout → acute pulmonary edema.
BP above about 180/120 with neuro change, chest pain, dyspnea, or falling urine output → hypertensive emergency.

topics.title: Health Promotion, Independent & Collaborative Interventions
topics.summary: Much cardiovascular disease is preventable; nurses teach risk reduction, arrange screening, and support circulation with monitoring, devices, and psychosocial care.

sections.heading: Risk factors and genetics
bullets: Nonmodifiable: age, gender, race, personal health history, and family history (high cholesterol, early-onset coronary artery disease).
Assess for manifestations suggesting a genetic disorder and refer for genetic testing, counseling, and evaluation.
Modifiable: smoking, unhealthy diet and high BMI, physical inactivity.
Secondary risk factors to control: high BP, high blood cholesterol, obesity, stress, and alcohol (abstain or drink only small amounts).

sections.heading: Lifestyle modifications
bullets: Quit smoking.
Proper nutrition — a heart-healthy diet low in saturated fat and sodium, rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.
Daily physical activity (e.g., at least 150 minutes/week of moderate activity).
Keep BMI below 25.
Reduce stress: exercise, relaxation techniques, biofeedback, therapeutic touch, yoga, meditation.

sections.heading: Screenings
bullets: BP screenings and monitoring of serum lipids.
ECG.
Stress tests — exercise or chemical; may be combined with a radionuclide test or stress echocardiography.
Electron beam CT to identify calcium blockages in the coronary arteries.

sections.heading: Independent nursing interventions
bullets: Support, improve, and promote adequate perfusion; goals depend on the disease process.
Teach primary prevention and lifestyle modification to reduce later risk.
Promote circulation and cardiopulmonary function: positioning, early ambulation, leg exercises.
Monitor inputs and outputs, daily weights, and continuous cardiac monitoring as ordered; trend vital signs and mental status.
Pressure supports and application/assessment of compression devices.
Psychosocial support — anxiety and depression are common with heart disease and stroke.
CPR (basic life support).

sections.heading: Collaborative therapies
bullets: Surgery and procedures (for example, opening or bypassing blocked arteries, valve repair).
Cardiac rehabilitation — supervised exercise, education, and counseling.
Pharmacologic therapy — e.g., medications to lower BP and cholesterol, prevent clots, and remove excess fluid.

Nonpharmacologic therapy: heart-healthy diet, nutritional and herbal supplements, weight loss, regular exercise, smoking cessation, stress reduction, drinking more water and less alcohol, compression stockings as needed, and chelation therapy (clients may use it — ask about all supplements and alternative therapies).

pearls: A teaching question with "BMI under 30" or "a few cigarettes a day is fine" is your "needs further teaching" answer — the goal is BMI <25 and no smoking.
You can't change age, gender, race, or family history — but you can change smoking, diet, weight, activity, BP, cholesterol, stress, and alcohol.
Ask about herbal and nutritional supplements — clients often don't think of them as "medications."
redFlags: Unresponsive client who is not breathing normally and has no pulse → call for help and start CPR immediately.

topics.title: Lifespan Considerations in Perfusion
topics.summary: Children, pregnant clients, and older adults each have unique normal findings and assessment techniques.

sections.heading: Infants and children
bullets: The heart is more sensitive to volume and pressure overload → greater risk of heart failure; cardiac function is affected by stress, exercise, fever, and respiratory distress.
Chronic hypoxemia → the bone marrow makes more RBCs (polycythemia).
Children respond to severe hypoxemia with bradycardia (adults respond with tachycardia) — bradycardia in a hypoxic child is an ominous sign.
Congenital heart disease is the leading cause of death (excluding prematurity) in the first year of life.
Pulse: use the apical pulse in infants and young children; peripheral or apical in preschoolers and older children. Newborns may have nonpathologic murmurs.
Count the pulse and take the BP before other procedures so discomfort does not artificially raise them.

sections.heading: Pediatric blood pressure
bullets: Infants: use palpation if auscultation with a stethoscope or Doppler is unsuccessful.
Arm and thigh pressures are equivalent in children younger than 1 year; after that, thigh pressure is about 10 mm Hg higher than arm pressure.
Measure BP in all children older than 3 years, and in younger children with certain medical conditions.
In children, the diastolic pressure is the onset of phase IV (sounds become muffled).

sections.heading: Pregnancy
bullets: Cardiac output increases early in pregnancy; at term, the pulse may increase by 10–15 bpm.
BP falls to its lowest point in the second trimester, then gradually rebounds.

Blood volume increases until about 30–34 weeks and plateaus at 40–50% above prepregnancy levels (more RBCs and plasma) to carry extra oxygen; the hematocrit decreases slightly, so dietary iron needs increase.
Leukocyte production increases — normal, and does not indicate infection.

Fibrin, fibrinogen, and factors VII, VIII, IX, and X increase; clotting time is about the same, but venous thrombosis risk rises. The enlarging uterus also slows venous return → blood stasis in the legs.

Supine hypotensive syndrome: lying supine lets the uterus press on the vena cava → less blood returns to the right atrium → low BP, dizziness, pallor, clamminess. Correct by turning the client onto her side or placing a pillow or wedge under the right hip.
An S3 may be heard in the third trimester (expected).

sections.heading: Older adults
bullets: Normal aging changes are hard to distinguish from disease; the capacity to adapt to cardiovascular stress decreases.
Atypical presentation: fatigue, decreased activity, sleep disturbance, and pain are not normal; mental status changes, agitation, or falls may be the first sign of a cardiac problem.
Heart: myocardial hypertrophy, stiff valves, slight decline in CO; fibrosis of the AV node → AV block; the stress of illness may trigger conduction problems.
Vessels: decreased elasticity ("hardening"), thickened intimal and medial layers, irregular endothelium, lipid deposits and calcification → elevated BP, sometimes isolated systolic hypertension.
Lungs: decreased chest wall compliance, increased AP diameter, airway closure in dependent areas, slightly lower PaO₂ — but an elevated PaCO₂ indicates pathology.
Kidneys: GFR falls 30–50% by age 80 → water retention and increased preload that can tax the heart, plus a decreased ability to concentrate urine → dehydration.
Pulse: radial may be hard to count with tremors (use apical); check pedal pulses for regularity, volume, and symmetry; the pulse returns to baseline more slowly after exercise.

BP: with arm contractures, assess by palpation with the arm relaxed or use the thigh; ask about antihypertensives; medications, dehydration, bleeding, burns, and some analgesics increase orthostatic hypotension — assess supine first, then sitting or standing.

table.caption: Quick comparison across the lifespan
rows: Severe hypoxemia → bradycardia; chronic hypoxemia → polycythemia
Apical pulse; count before procedures; arm = thigh BP under 1 year
Blood volume +40–50%; slight Hct drop; more clotting factors
Avoid lying flat late in pregnancy — side-lying or wedge under right hip
Stiff arteries, AV node fibrosis, lower GFR
Apical pulse if tremors; palpate or use thigh with contractures; check orthostatic BP

pearls: Pregnant client dizzy and pale while supine → turn her onto her side before anything else.
A hypoxic child who becomes bradycardic is about to arrest — escalate immediately.
In older adults, a new fall or confusion is a perfusion assessment trigger, not just a safety event.
redFlags: Bradycardia in a hypoxemic infant or child.
Unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and pain in a pregnant client (hypercoagulable state).
Sudden confusion, agitation, or falls in an older adult with cardiac history.

flashcards.back: Mainly during diastole — so tachycardia reduces coronary perfusion

Injury or disease of the limb, cast/bulky bandage, axillary (or hip) lymph node removal on that side, IV infusion, AV fistula

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Sounds & Cardiac Auscultation
questions.hintContent: Recall which chamber forms the apex, where the normal PMI sits, and where blood backs up when each side of the heart fails.
questions.hintStrategy: First decide which chamber the PMI finding points to, then check whether the lung finding fits that same side of the heart.
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with long-standing heart failure and an ejection fraction of 30% is having a cardiac assessment. The nurse palpates the point of maximal impulse (PMI) at the 6th intercostal space, left anterior axillary line; it is diffuse and about 4 cm wide. Fine crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which interpretation best connects these findings?
options: An enlarged left ventricle has shifted the apex, and blood is backing up into the lungs
An enlarged right ventricle has shifted the apex, and blood is backing up into the lungs
The apex is in a normal location for age, and the crackles reflect aging airways
Fluid in the pericardial cavity has moved the apex, and it is compressing the lungs
optionRationales: Correct. The apex is formed by the left ventricle, so a PMI displaced down and to the left and wider than a coin suggests left ventricular enlargement. A failing left ventricle backs blood up into the pulmonary circulation, producing crackles.
Incorrect. The apex (and PMI) reflects the left ventricle, and right-sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins (JVD, edema), not the lungs.
Incorrect. At any adult age the normal PMI is a small tap at the 5th ICS, left midclavicular line. Crackles in a client with heart failure point to fluid, not normal aging.
Incorrect. Pericardial fluid squeezes the heart and limits filling; it does not produce a displaced, diffuse PMI, and crackles come from fluid in the alveoli.
questions.rationale: Two pieces of anatomy explain this picture. The left ventricle forms the apex, which normally taps the chest wall as a small (coin-sized) PMI at the 5th ICS, left midclavicular line. A dilated left ventricle — common with a low ejection fraction — pushes the apex down and laterally and spreads the impulse out. Because the pulmonary and systemic circulations are connected in series, a failing left ventricle backs blood up into the lungs, which is why crackles accompany the displaced PMI.
questions.takeaway: PMI shifted down/left and diffuse = enlarged left ventricle; left-sided failure backs up into the lungs.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Sounds & Cardiac Auscultation
questions.hintContent: Connect the timing of S3 vs. S4, the meaning of excess preload, and the signs of fluid overload in heart failure.
questions.hintStrategy: Name the sound from its timing first, then use the weight change and sleeping position to decide whether it is expected or a warning.
questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with heart failure has gained 2 kg since yesterday and now needs three pillows to sleep. With the bell at the apex, the nurse hears a new low-pitched sound immediately after S2 that creates a "Ken-TUC-ky" cadence. How should the nurse interpret this sound?
options: An S4 from the atrium pushing blood into a stiff, thickened ventricle
An S3 from rapid filling of a ventricle overstretched by excess preload
A split S2 from the pulmonic valve closing late during inspiration
An S3 that is an expected finding because the ventricles stiffen with aging
optionRationales: Incorrect. An S4 occurs just before S1 ("TEN-nes-see"), not right after S2, and reflects a stiff ventricle rather than volume overload.

Correct. A sound right after S2 is an S3 (early diastole). With new weight gain and orthopnea, it signals rapid filling of a volume-overloaded ventricle — too much preload, which makes a weak heart contract less effectively.
Incorrect. A physiologic split S2 is heard best at the pulmonic area with the diaphragm and comes and goes with breathing; it is not a low-pitched apical gallop.
Incorrect. S3 can be normal in children, young adults, and third-trimester pregnancy — not in an older adult with heart failure, and stiffening is linked to S4, not S3.
questions.rationale: Timing identifies the sound: right after S2 in early diastole = S3 (ventricular gallop). Context gives the meaning. This client has heart failure plus a 2-kg overnight gain and new orthopnea — signs of fluid overload. Excess volume raises preload, and continuous overstretching of the fibers makes contraction less effective, so blood rushing into the already-full ventricle produces the S3. Together these cues point to worsening heart failure that needs to be reported.
questions.takeaway: New S3 + weight gain + orthopnea in heart failure = volume overload (too much preload); report it.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Heart Sounds & Cardiac Auscultation
questions.hintContent: Link who may normally have an S3 to the cardiovascular changes of pregnancy (blood volume, pulse, position).
questions.hintStrategy: Check every finding against what is expected at 35 weeks; look for any sign of fluid in the lungs before deciding to escalate.
questions.stem: A healthy 26-year-old client at 35 weeks' gestation has an S3 heart sound. Her BP is 112/68 mm Hg and pulse is 92/min (prepregnancy pulse 78/min); RR is 18/min, SpO₂ is 99%, and her lungs are clear. Which action is most important for the nurse to take?
options: Notify the provider that the S3 and faster pulse suggest heart failure
Restrict oral fluids to reduce the extra circulating blood volume
Document the S3 and pulse as expected third-trimester findings
Have her lie flat on her back and recheck the heart sounds
optionRationales: Incorrect. Without dyspnea, crackles, or low SpO₂, these are normal adaptations of pregnancy, not signs of heart failure.
Incorrect. The increased blood volume is a normal, needed change that supports the mother and fetus; fluid restriction is not indicated.

Correct. Blood volume rises 40–50% by late pregnancy and the pulse rises 10–15/min by term, so an S3 with normal vital signs and clear lungs is expected. Documenting it avoids unnecessary intervention.
Incorrect. Lying supine late in pregnancy lets the uterus compress the vena cava, which can cause supine hypotensive syndrome.
questions.rationale: An S3 comes from rapid filling of a very compliant ventricle when blood volume is high, which is why it can be normal in the third trimester. Pregnancy also raises cardiac output and the pulse (up 10–15/min by term), and blood volume plateaus 40–50% above prepregnancy levels. With a normal BP, a pulse only 14/min above baseline, SpO₂ 99%, and clear lungs, both findings are expected and should be documented. The same S3 with crackles or dyspnea would need follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Third-trimester S3 and a pulse up 10–15/min with normal findings = expected; document it.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload & Contractility
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Connect peripheral vascular resistance (a BP determinant) with afterload and myocardial oxygen demand.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify which determinant an arterial drug changes, then follow that change to the work the left ventricle must do.
questions.stem: A client with hypertension (BP 164/96 mm Hg) and heart failure is started on an arterial vasodilator. The client asks, "How does lowering my blood pressure help my heart?" Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "Relaxing the veins sends more blood back to your heart, so it stretches more and beats harder."
"Widening the arteries lets your heart muscle squeeze harder, so it pumps more blood each minute."
"Lowering your pressure slows your heart through your nerves, so it has more time to rest."
"Relaxing the arteries lowers resistance, so your heart pumps against less force and works less."
optionRationales: Incorrect. This describes increased preload; an arterial vasodilator acts mainly on resistance (afterload), and more preload would burden a failing heart.
Incorrect. Vasodilators do not directly increase contractility; they reduce the resistance the ventricle must overcome.
Incorrect. When BP falls, baroreceptor reflexes tend to speed the heart, not slow it.
Correct. Arterial vasodilation lowers peripheral vascular resistance, which lowers both BP and afterload. Less afterload means less workload and lower myocardial oxygen demand.
questions.rationale: Peripheral vascular resistance is one of the four determinants of BP, and it is also the main driver of afterload — the force the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. High afterload raises myocardial oxygen consumption and can start a vicious cycle in a failing heart. An arterial vasodilator relaxes arterial tone, lowering resistance, BP, and afterload together, so the heart does less work.
questions.takeaway: Arterial vasodilator: ↓ resistance → ↓ BP and ↓ afterload → ↓ cardiac workload and O₂ demand.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload & Contractility
questions.hintContent: Relate heart rate to diastolic filling time, stroke volume, and what the radial pulse represents.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask what a very fast rate does to ventricular filling, then apply that same idea to why some beats are not felt at the wrist.
questions.stem: A client with atrial fibrillation has an apical rate of 156/min and a simultaneous radial rate of 118/min. BP has fallen from 128/76 to 88/54 mm Hg, and the client reports lightheadedness. Which explanation best accounts for both the low BP and the difference between the two rates?
options: Shortened diastole limits filling, so stroke volume falls and some beats never reach the wrist
The fast rate raises afterload, so the ventricle cannot eject and the radial artery constricts
The fast rate creates excess preload, so the overstretched ventricle ejects too weakly
The fast rate triggers vagal vasodilation, so BP falls and the radial pulse is hard to feel
optionRationales: Correct. At very fast rates the ventricles cannot fill, so stroke volume, cardiac output, and BP fall. Beats with very little stroke volume are heard at the apex but not felt at the radial artery — a pulse deficit of 38.
Incorrect. The problem is loss of filling time, not increased resistance to ejection; a pulse deficit reflects weak beats, not radial constriction.
Incorrect. A rapid rate reduces preload by shortening filling time; it does not overfill the ventricle.
Incorrect. Vagal tone slows the heart; it is not the cause of hypotension in a rapid rhythm, and it does not explain a pulse deficit.
questions.rationale: Cardiac output = HR × SV, but heart rate helps only up to a point. At 156/min, diastole is so short that the ventricles do not fill, so stroke volume falls and CO and BP drop. The pulse is the wave of blood from each left ventricular contraction; beats with too little stroke volume do not produce a palpable radial pulse, creating a pulse deficit (156 − 118 = 38). Both findings come from the same loss of filling time.
questions.takeaway: Very fast rate → lost filling time → ↓ SV, ↓ CO/BP, and a pulse deficit.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Conduction System & Action Potential
questions.hintContent: Match each ECG interval to a part of the conduction pathway, and recall how aging changes the AV node.
questions.hintStrategy: Find the one measurement that is abnormal, locate its part of the pathway, then consider the client's age.
questions.stem: A 79-year-old client takes a medication that slows the heart rate. The heart rate is 58/min. The rhythm strip shows a P wave before every QRS complex, a PR interval of 0.28 seconds (previously 0.18 seconds), and a QRS of 0.08 seconds. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: Conduction is slowed in the SA node, which is a normal effect of aging on the pacemaker
Conduction is slowed in the AV node, and age-related AV node fibrosis may contribute
Conduction is slowed in the bundle branches, which explains the lengthened PR interval
Conduction is slowed in the Purkinje fibers, which will soon widen the QRS complex
optionRationales: Incorrect. The SA node's firing is reflected by the P wave, which is present before every QRS; the lengthened interval is after the P wave.

Correct. The PR interval measures travel through the AV node; 0.28 seconds is prolonged. Aging causes fibrosis of the AV node, which can lead to AV block, and heart-rate–slowing medications can add to the delay.
Incorrect. Bundle branch problems widen the QRS (0.12 seconds or more); this QRS of 0.08 seconds is normal.
Incorrect. The normal QRS shows ventricular conduction is intact; the PR interval points to the AV node.
questions.rationale: The ECG maps onto the pathway: P wave = atrial depolarization, PR interval = time through the AV node (normal 0.12–0.20 s), QRS = bundle branches and Purkinje fibers (normal < 0.12 s). A PR of 0.28 s with a normal QRS places the delay in the AV node. In older adults, fibrosis of the AV node can cause AV block, and the stress of illness or heart-rate–lowering drugs can bring conduction problems to light.
questions.takeaway: Long PR + normal QRS = AV node delay; aging (AV node fibrosis) raises the risk of AV block.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Consider how cuff size affects the reading, the client's baseline, and what defines a hypertensive emergency.
questions.hintStrategy: Before escalating or treating, ask whether the number itself can be trusted.
questions.stem: A client with an arm circumference of 42 cm has a BP of 168/96 mm Hg measured with a standard adult cuff. Previous readings were 124/78 to 130/80 mm Hg. The client denies headache, chest pain, vision changes, and shortness of breath. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider of a possible hypertensive emergency
Recheck the BP in the same arm right away with the same cuff
Remeasure the BP with a large adult cuff after a brief rest
Give the PRN antihypertensive and recheck the BP in 1 hour
optionRationales: Incorrect. A hypertensive emergency requires severe BP with acute organ damage; this client has no symptoms, and the reading is likely a cuff error.
Incorrect. Repeating immediately on the same arm with the wrong cuff repeats the error and gives an inaccurate reading.
Correct. A cuff too small for the arm reads falsely high. When a reading does not fit the client's baseline, verify it with correct technique before acting.
Incorrect. Treating a likely false reading could cause hypotension; the value must be verified first.
questions.rationale: A cuff that is too small must squeeze harder to occlude the artery and reads falsely high. This reading is far above the client's baseline, and there are no signs of target-organ damage (headache, chest pain, vision change, dyspnea), so it does not suggest a hypertensive emergency — which is defined by organ damage, not the number. The first action is to verify with a correctly sized cuff after rest.
questions.takeaway: Unexpected high BP with the wrong cuff → verify with the right cuff first; emergencies are defined by organ damage.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Connect the auscultatory gap technique with pulse pressure and the vascular changes of aging.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the systolic and adult diastolic values first, then calculate the pulse pressure and ask what explains it at this age.
questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with long-standing hypertension has a palpated systolic estimate of 186 mm Hg. After inflating the cuff to 216 mm Hg, the nurse hears the first tapping at 184 mm Hg. The sounds disappear at 166, reappear at 148, and disappear completely at 86 mm Hg. Which statement correctly records and interprets this reading?
options: 148/86 with a gap from 166 to 148; the pulse pressure is normal for age
184/166 with no gap; the narrow pulse pressure fits a low stroke volume
166/86 with a gap from 184 to 166; the pulse pressure is normal for age
184/86, gap 166 to 148; the wide pulse pressure fits stiff arteries
optionRationales: Incorrect. The sounds that return after an auscultatory gap are not the systolic; recording 148 misses significant hypertension.
Incorrect. The first silence is the auscultatory gap, not the diastolic pressure; adult diastolic is phase V (final silence).
Incorrect. The first sound heard (184) is the systolic value, and the gap was between 166 and 148.
Correct. Systolic is the first sound (184) and adult diastolic is the final silence (86). The pulse pressure of 98 mm Hg is wide, consistent with loss of arterial elasticity in older adults.
questions.rationale: Palpating first and inflating 30 mm Hg above the estimate lets the nurse hear the true first sound (184) above an auscultatory gap, which is common in older adults with hypertension and stiff arteries. The BP is recorded as 184/86 with the gap noted. Age-related loss of arterial elasticity raises resistance so systolic spikes while diastolic stays normal or low, giving a wide pulse pressure (184 − 86 = 98) — the pattern of isolated systolic hypertension.
questions.takeaway: Auscultatory gap: SBP = first sound, DBP = final silence; wide pulse pressure in older adults reflects stiff arteries.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall the five Korotkoff phases and how the diastolic endpoint differs between adults and children.
questions.hintStrategy: Assign systolic first, then decide which diastolic phase applies to this age group.
questions.stem: The nurse measures the blood pressure of a calm 9-year-old child with a correctly sized arm cuff. The first clear tapping is heard at 104 mm Hg, the sounds become muffled at 62 mm Hg, and they disappear at 54 mm Hg. How should the nurse record this blood pressure?
options: 104/62, because muffling marks diastolic pressure in children
104/54, because silence marks diastolic pressure at every age
62/54, because muffling and silence together mark the range
104/58, because diastolic is averaged between the two points
optionRationales: Correct. In children, the diastolic pressure is the onset of phase IV (muffling), so the reading is 104/62.
Incorrect. Phase V (silence) is used for diastolic in adults; in children the onset of muffling (phase IV) is used.
Incorrect. Systolic pressure is always the first clear tapping (phase I), here 104 mm Hg.
Incorrect. Korotkoff phases are not averaged; a specific phase is recorded as the diastolic value.
questions.rationale: Korotkoff phase I (first tapping) is the systolic pressure at every age. The diastolic differs by age: adults use phase V (disappearance), while children use the onset of phase IV (muffling). This child's BP is therefore 104/62. BP is measured in all children older than 3 years, ideally before other procedures so discomfort does not raise it.
questions.takeaway: Adults: phase I / phase V. Children: phase I / phase IV (muffling).

questions.hintContent: Link diuretic effects on blood volume and preload to what happens to BP and brain perfusion on standing.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client shows signs of fainting, choose the action that protects the client immediately over data collection or calls.
questions.stem: A client receiving furosemide reports dizziness when getting out of bed, and the nurse is measuring orthostatic vital signs. Supine readings were BP 128/78 mm Hg, P 76/min. After 1 minute of standing, the client grips the bedrail, turns pale, and says, "Everything is going gray." Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Steady the client and complete the 3-minute standing reading
Help the client sit or lie back down on the bed at once
Give the client an oral fluid bolus to replace diuresed volume
Call the provider to request holding the next diuretic dose
optionRationales: Incorrect. Keeping a symptomatic client upright risks syncope and a fall; finishing the numbers is not the priority.
Correct. The client is symptomatic, so safety comes first. Lying down restores blood flow to the brain and prevents a fall; the symptoms themselves are a positive finding to document and report.
Incorrect. Fluids do not act fast enough to prevent a faint, and the client must be lowered first.
Incorrect. Reporting is appropriate after the client is safe; the nurse does not leave a near-syncopal client standing.
questions.rationale: A diuretic lowers blood volume and therefore preload, so less blood returns to the heart when the client stands; stroke volume and BP fall and brain perfusion drops. Graying vision and pallor mean the client is about to faint. During orthostatic testing, a symptomatic client is returned to bed right away — the symptoms confirm the problem even without the final numbers. Reporting and medication review follow once the client is safe.
questions.takeaway: Diuretic → ↓ preload → orthostatic drop; if symptoms appear during testing, lower the client first.

questions.hintContent: Connect the pulse deficit calculation with what the pulse represents and how an irregular rhythm affects ventricular filling.
questions.hintStrategy: Calculate the difference first, then explain why a beat heard at the apex might not be felt at the wrist.
questions.stem: Two nurses assess a client with a new irregular rhythm simultaneously for 1 full minute. The apical rate is 110/min and the radial rate is 92/min. What is the best interpretation of this finding?
options: A counting error; the apical and radial rates should always be identical
A normal finding; the radial artery is too far away to transmit every beat
A pulse deficit of 18; early beats have too little volume to reach the wrist
A pulse deficit of 18; the radial rate is more accurate and is documented alone
optionRationales: Incorrect. The rates are normally identical, but a difference in an irregular rhythm is a real pulse deficit, not necessarily an error.
Incorrect. In a healthy person every heartbeat produces a palpable pulse; a deficit is abnormal and should be reported.

Correct. Apical − radial = 18. With an irregular rhythm, some beats occur before the ventricles have filled, so their stroke volume is too small to create a palpable radial pulse; those beats are not perfusing the body.
Incorrect. The apical rate is the more accurate count of heartbeats; both rates and the deficit are documented and reported.
questions.rationale: The pulse is the wave of blood created by left ventricular contraction and represents stroke volume. In an irregular rhythm, some impulses arrive before the ventricles have filled, so those contractions eject too little blood to be felt at the wrist, although they are heard at the apex. The difference between the simultaneous apical and radial rates (110 − 92 = 18) is the pulse deficit, meaning 18 beats a minute are not perfusing the periphery.
questions.takeaway: Pulse deficit = apical − radial; early beats with low stroke volume do not reach the wrist.

questions.hintContent: Relate the 0–4+ pulse scale to stroke volume and the effect of blood loss on preload.
questions.hintStrategy: Grade the pulse from the description, then check which explanation fits a bleeding client with a fast heart rate.
questions.stem: A client admitted with black, tarry stools has HR 122/min, BP 98/80 mm Hg, and cool feet. The nurse palpates the dorsalis pedis pulse and finds it faint and easily obliterated with light pressure. Which documentation and interpretation are most accurate?
options: 4+, reflecting a bounding pulse from sympathetic stimulation
2+, reflecting a normal volume maintained by the fast heart rate
3+, reflecting a full pulse from the compensatory tachycardia
1+, reflecting a reduced stroke volume from blood loss
optionRationales: Incorrect. A 4+ pulse is bounding and cannot be obliterated; it is associated with fluid overload, not blood loss.
Incorrect. A 2+ pulse is easily felt and not easily obliterated; this pulse is diminished.
Incorrect. A 3+ pulse is full and increased (for example, with exercise or fever), which does not fit a faint pulse.
Correct. A weak, thready pulse that disappears with light pressure is 1+. Blood loss lowers preload and stroke volume, so each pulse wave is small despite the fast heart rate.
questions.rationale: Pulse volume reflects stroke volume. A pulse that is faint and easily obliterated is graded 1+ (diminished). Here, blood loss from GI bleeding lowers preload, so stroke volume falls; the heart speeds up to protect cardiac output, but each beat still delivers a weak pulse. The narrowed pulse pressure (18 mm Hg) and cool feet support reduced perfusion.
questions.takeaway: Weak, easily obliterated pulse = 1+; with bleeding it reflects ↓ preload and ↓ stroke volume.

questions.hintContent: Connect where the jugular veins drain, which circulation each ventricle backs into, and how left-sided failure leads to right-sided failure.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide which side of the heart the neck and ankle findings point to, then consider how the client's history led there.
questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with long-standing left-sided heart failure is assessed with the head of the bed at 45°. The internal jugular pulsation is visible 7 cm above the sternal angle, and both ankles have 2+ pitting edema. Which explanation is most consistent with these findings?
options: Right-sided failure, which is most often caused by left-sided failure
Hypovolemia from diuretics, which makes the neck veins distend to compensate
Peripheral arterial disease, which reduces arterial flow to both lower legs
Isolated left-sided failure, which backs fluid directly into the neck veins
optionRationales: Correct. JVD and dependent edema mean blood is backing up into the systemic veins behind a failing right ventricle. The most common cause of right-sided failure is left-sided failure.
Incorrect. Low volume makes the neck veins flat, not distended, and does not cause pitting edema.
Incorrect. Arterial disease causes cool, pale, hairless legs with weak pulses, not JVD with pitting edema.
Incorrect. Left-sided failure backs blood into the lungs (crackles, dyspnea); the jugular veins drain into the right heart.
questions.rationale: The jugular veins drain directly into the right atrium. A pulsation more than about 3–4 cm above the sternal angle at 30–45° is JVD, and together with dependent pitting edema it shows blood backing up into the systemic veins — the circuit behind the right ventricle. Because the circulations are in series, a long-standing failing left ventricle raises pressures in the lungs and eventually overloads the right ventricle, making left-sided failure the most common cause of right-sided failure.
questions.takeaway: JVD + dependent edema = right-sided backup; left-sided failure is its most common cause.

questions.hintContent: Connect the steps of hemostasis and fibrinolysis with the drug classes that act on each, and with what is happening in an ischemic stroke.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the drug to the step it affects, then choose the monitoring that fits that drug's main risk.
questions.stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke is receiving IV alteplase. The client's daughter asks, "How is this medicine supposed to help my mom, and what are you watching for?" Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "It keeps her platelets from clumping; I will watch for a new clot forming in her legs."
"It turns on the enzyme that dissolves clots; I will watch for bleeding or a new headache."
"It slows her clotting factors; I will watch for the clot in her brain to grow larger."
"It thins her blood around the clot; I will watch for her blood pressure to climb too high."
optionRationales: Incorrect. This describes an antiplatelet such as aspirin, which weakens the platelet plug but does not dissolve an existing clot.

Correct. Alteplase is manufactured tPA, which activates plasmin to digest fibrin and dissolve the clot blocking brain blood flow. Its main risk is bleeding, including in the brain, so new headache or neuro change is reported at once.
Incorrect. This describes an anticoagulant, which prevents clot growth but does not dissolve the clot already present.
Incorrect. Thrombolytics do not "thin" blood; they break down fibrin. Bleeding, not rising BP, is the key danger to monitor.
questions.rationale: In an ischemic stroke, a clot — often from atrial fibrillation — blocks a brain artery, and brain tissue dies within minutes. Fibrinolysis normally dissolves clots when tPA activates plasmin, which digests fibrin. Alteplase is manufactured tPA, so it speeds this process to restore blood flow. Because it dissolves clots, its main danger is bleeding, so the nurse watches for new headache, neurologic changes, or bleeding and reports them immediately.
questions.takeaway: Alteplase (tPA) → plasmin dissolves the stroke clot; watch for bleeding and neuro change.

questions.hintContent: Connect risk factors for venous thrombosis, side-to-side leg assessment, and the safety rules for compression devices.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the one client whose assessment already suggests a clot rather than just a risk for one.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing clients who have prescriptions for sequential compression devices (SCDs). For which client is it most important for the nurse to withhold the SCD and immediately contact the provider?
options: A client on bed rest after a stroke who has intact skin and 2+ pedal pulses bilaterally
A client at 36 weeks' gestation on bed rest whose clotting time is normal and legs are equal
A client 2 days after hip replacement whose left calf is newly swollen, warm, and tender
A client receiving a daily anticoagulant injection who says the sleeves make her legs sweaty
optionRationales: Incorrect. Symmetric pulses and intact skin are expected; this immobile client benefits from the SCD.
Incorrect. Pregnancy raises venous thrombosis risk even with a normal clotting time, but equal legs show no sign of a clot, so compression is appropriate.
Correct. New one-sided swelling, warmth, and tenderness suggest a venous clot. Compressing that leg could dislodge it, so the device is withheld and the provider notified.
Incorrect. Sweating is a comfort issue to address; anticoagulant therapy is not a reason to withhold an SCD.
questions.rationale: Venous stasis from immobility and the clotting changes of pregnancy both raise the risk of venous thrombosis, which is why SCDs are ordered. Before compressing, the nurse assesses the legs: comparing side to side, a newly swollen, warm, tender calf on one side suggests a clot already exists. Squeezing that leg could break the clot loose, so the SCD is withheld and the provider notified. The other clients show no signs of a clot and should keep their devices.
questions.takeaway: Assess before compressing: new one-sided calf swelling, warmth, tenderness → withhold and notify.

questions.hintContent: Recall what troponin measures and how quickly it rises after heart muscle injury.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider the timing of the blood draw relative to the start of symptoms.
questions.stem: A client arrives in the emergency department 1 hour after the onset of substernal chest pressure. The initial troponin level is within normal limits. The client asks, "Does this mean I didn't have a heart attack?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Yes — a normal troponin shows no damage, so you should be able to go home."
"Not exactly — troponin reflects leg muscle damage, so we will order another test."
"Not really — the ECG is what matters, so the blood test result is not important."
"Not yet — troponin takes a few hours to rise, so the test will be repeated."
optionRationales: Incorrect. A single early normal troponin cannot rule out a heart attack.
Incorrect. Troponin is the most specific marker of heart muscle injury.
Incorrect. The ECG and cardiac markers answer different questions; serial troponins remain important.
Correct. Troponin is released as heart muscle is injured and takes hours to rise, so one early normal value does not rule out injury; serial draws are needed.
questions.rationale: Injured myocardial cells leak proteins such as troponin into the blood, but the level takes a few hours to rise after injury begins. A value drawn 1 hour after symptom onset may still be normal even if a heart attack is occurring, so the provider orders serial troponins to look for a rise.
questions.takeaway: One early normal troponin never rules out MI — trend serial values.

questions.hintContent: Connect the risks after femoral catheterization with the early signs of volume loss in pulse pressure and heart rate.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether the client is actively losing blood; if so, choose the action that stops the loss before assessing further.
questions.stem: Two hours after a cardiac catheterization via the right femoral artery, the client says, "My groin suddenly feels warm and wet." HR has risen from 84 to 106/min, and BP has changed from 126/78 to 108/88 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply firm, direct pressure just above the puncture site
Check the right pedal pulse and compare it with the left
Repeat a full set of vital signs to confirm the trend
Raise the head of the bed to 90° to inspect the site
optionRationales: Correct. The sensation plus a rising heart rate and a narrowing pulse pressure (20 mm Hg) signal arterial bleeding. Stopping the bleeding comes first; then call for help and reassess.
Incorrect. Distal pulse checks are needed, but not before controlling active bleeding.
Incorrect. The trend already suggests volume loss; delaying pressure allows more blood loss.
Incorrect. Sitting up bends the groin and can worsen bleeding; the head of the bed stays at 30° or less after femoral access.
questions.rationale: After femoral catheterization, bleeding from the arterial puncture is a major risk. A warm, wet groin together with a rising heart rate and a narrowing pulse pressure (systolic falling while diastolic stays up as vessels constrict) indicates volume loss. Firm pressure just above the puncture site — where the artery was entered — stops the bleeding; the nurse then calls for help, checks pulses and vital signs, and notifies the provider.
questions.takeaway: Warm, wet groin + rising HR + narrowing pulse pressure after cath → pressure above the site first.

questions.hintContent: Link the main risks of contrast dye to normal age-related changes in kidney function.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask which result could turn into harm from the procedure itself, then weigh the other findings against what is normal for age.
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the data of an 81-year-old client scheduled for cardiac catheterization with contrast in 2 hours. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report to the provider before the procedure?
options: BP 148/76 mm Hg
Serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL
Potassium 4.2 mEq/L
NPO since midnight except sips with medications
optionRationales: Incorrect. A mildly elevated systolic with a normal diastolic is common in older adults with stiff arteries and does not need to be reported before the cath.
Correct. Contrast dye can injure the kidneys, and kidney function already declines with age (GFR falls 30–50% by 80). An elevated creatinine must be reported before the procedure.
Incorrect. This potassium is within normal limits.
Incorrect. This is expected preparation for the procedure.
questions.rationale: Before catheterization, the nurse checks kidney function because contrast dye can cause kidney injury. In older adults, the glomerular filtration rate is already reduced by 30–50% by age 80, so a creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL signals kidneys at high risk and must be reported before the dye is given. The BP pattern reflects age-related arterial stiffening, and the other findings are normal or expected.
questions.takeaway: Contrast + elevated creatinine (especially with age-reduced GFR) → report before the cath.

questions.hintContent: Connect BE-FAST findings, the source of a clot in atrial fibrillation, and the time-dependence of clot-dissolving treatment.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the information that directly changes what treatment can be given in the next few minutes.
questions.stem: B.E., a 64-year-old man with CAD, hypertension, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and diabetes, arrives in the emergency department after collapsing at home. His wife reports that before he lost consciousness he was confused, had left-arm numbness and double vision, slurred speech, and left facial droop. He is now awake. Which information is most important for the nurse to obtain from the wife immediately?
options: Whether he takes a daily low-dose aspirin
The name of his outpatient cardiologist
The exact time he was last seen normal
Whether he follows a low-sodium diet
optionRationales: Incorrect. Medication history matters, but it does not come before establishing the time last known well.
Incorrect. This can be obtained later; it does not affect immediate stroke treatment.
Correct. Eligibility for clot-dissolving therapy (tPA) depends on how much time has passed since he was last known well.
Incorrect. Diet history does not guide emergency stroke care.
questions.rationale: Sudden one-sided face droop, arm numbness, double vision, and slurred speech are BE-FAST signs; with atrial fibrillation as a clot source, this is treated as an ischemic stroke. Because "time is brain," the treatment decision — including a thrombolytic that activates plasmin to dissolve the clot — depends on the time last known well, so it is the first question to ask.
questions.takeaway: Suspected stroke: "When was he last known well?" guides clot-dissolving therapy.
