questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Consider how stroke affects swallowing and airway protection.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the option that prevents aspiration rather than the one that relieves thirst.
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is being evaluated for an acute stroke; he has slurred speech and left facial droop. He tells the nurse he is very thirsty and asks for a cup of water. Which action is the nurse's priority?
options: Give water through a straw so he can control the amount
Offer a cup of ice chips instead of water to relieve thirst
Provide thickened water with him sitting fully upright
Explain he must stay NPO until a swallow screen is passed
optionRationales: Incorrect. A straw does not protect the airway, and his swallow has not been screened.
Incorrect. Ice chips melt into water and carry the same aspiration risk.
Incorrect. Any oral intake, even thickened, waits until the swallow screen is passed.
Correct. Stroke can weaken the muscles used to swallow, so even a sip could be aspirated. He stays NPO until a bedside swallow screen is passed; mouth care can ease thirst.
questions.rationale: Slurred speech and facial droop suggest the stroke may affect the muscles of swallowing. Until a bedside swallow screen is passed, the client stays NPO to prevent aspiration and pneumonia. The nurse acknowledges his thirst and may offer mouth care.
questions.takeaway: Suspected stroke → NPO until a swallow screen is passed, even if thirsty.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Stroke, Heart Failure, Pulmonary Edema & Hypertensive Crisis
questions.hintContent: Connect low urine output to cardiac output, fluid overload to lung findings, and airway priorities after stroke.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply airway-breathing-circulation, and ask whether the low urine output means too little fluid or too weak a pump.
questions.stem: B.E., 64, who has a history of heart failure, is in the ICU 36 hours after an ischemic stroke. He has bilateral crackles (worse on the right), pooled oral secretions, SpO₂ 87% on a nonrebreather mask, RR 30/min, pitting edema of the legs, and urine output of 15 mL/h. He is difficult to arouse. The provider and respiratory therapist have been called. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Raise the head of the bed and suction the oropharynx
Infuse a 500-mL normal saline bolus for the low urine output
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to measure output
Obtain a daily weight using the bed scale
optionRationales: Correct. Clearing the airway and sitting him up let oxygen reach the lungs, help the lungs expand, and reduce venous return to an overloaded heart.
Incorrect. The low output reflects poor cardiac output with fluid overload, not dehydration; a bolus would worsen the pulmonary congestion.
Incorrect. Accurate I&O matters, but it does not address the failing airway and oxygenation.
Incorrect. Daily weight tracks fluid status but is not the first action for a client with hypoxemia and pooled secretions.
questions.rationale: Crackles, leg edema, and oliguria in a client with heart failure mean fluid overload with a heart that cannot keep up; the kidneys are underperfused because cardiac output is low, not because he is dry. Pooled secretions and a weak cough add aspiration risk, and falling SpO₂ with decreasing responsiveness signals impending respiratory failure. Airway comes first: raise the head of the bed and suction. A fluid bolus would add preload to a failing heart and worsen the lungs.
questions.takeaway: Crackles + edema + low urine output = low CO with fluid overload → airway and position first; no fluid bolus.

questions.hintContent: Connect the position of the pregnant uterus, venous return (preload), and cardiac output.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify what is blocking blood from returning to the heart, then choose the action that removes that cause.
questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks' gestation lying flat for an ultrasound reports feeling dizzy and nauseated. She is pale and clammy, and her BP is 88/50 mm Hg (baseline 114/70). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Turn the client onto her left side
Increase the rate of the IV fluid infusion
Elevate both legs on pillows while supine
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tilting her head down while still supine leaves the uterus compressing the vena cava.
Correct. Lifting the uterus off the vena cava restores venous return and preload, so cardiac output and BP recover. Then recheck the BP.
Incorrect. The problem is obstructed venous return, not low volume; repositioning corrects it faster.
Incorrect. Leg elevation cannot overcome compression of the vena cava by the uterus while she remains flat.
questions.rationale: Late in pregnancy, the heavy uterus compresses the vena cava when the client lies supine. Less blood returns to the right atrium, so preload, stroke volume, cardiac output, and BP fall, producing dizziness, pallor, and clamminess — supine hypotensive syndrome. Turning her to the side (or placing a wedge under the right hip) relieves the compression and is done before anything else.
questions.takeaway: Supine hypotensive syndrome: vena cava compression → ↓ preload → ↓ BP; turn her to the side first.

questions.hintContent: Connect the limbs to avoid for BP measurement with the age-specific arm–thigh relationship in children.
questions.hintStrategy: Confirm the site choice was correct, then compare the numbers using the rule for this age.
questions.stem: A 5-year-old child has casts on both forearms after a fall, so the nurse measures the blood pressure on the thigh with a correctly sized cuff. The thigh reading is 112/64 mm Hg. The child's arm BP at a clinic visit last month was 102/62 mm Hg, and the child is calm and playing. How should the nurse interpret and document this reading?
options: Elevated — report the rise and arrange a hypertension evaluation today
Unreliable — remeasure on an arm over the cast using a smaller cuff
Expected — document it as a thigh reading, about 10 mm Hg higher
Inaccurate — arm and thigh pressures should match at this age
optionRationales: Incorrect. The difference matches the expected thigh–arm gap in children over 1 year.
Incorrect. BP is never measured on a limb with a cast.
Correct. Casts rule out both arms, so the thigh is the right site. After age 1, thigh pressure is about 10 mm Hg higher than arm pressure; documenting the site lets others compare like with like.
Incorrect. Arm and thigh pressures are equivalent only in children younger than 1 year.
questions.rationale: A limb with a cast is not used for BP, so the thigh is the appropriate alternative for this child. In children older than 1 year, thigh pressure is about 10 mm Hg higher than arm pressure (under 1 year they are equal). A thigh reading of 112/64 compared with an arm reading of 102/62 is therefore expected, and the site is documented.
questions.takeaway: Casts rule out the arms; in a child over 1 year, thigh BP ≈ 10 mm Hg higher — document the site.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Connect the orthostatic hypotension criteria (systolic or diastolic drop within 3 minutes of standing) with what the lessons say is a leading cause of positional BP drops in older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: First do the math on the supine and standing readings and decide whether criteria are met; then choose the follow-up question that explains the finding and could change the plan.
questions.stem: An 81-year-old client reports feeling lightheaded when getting out of bed in the morning and has fallen once this week. Supine BP is 142/80 mm Hg; after 1 minute of standing it is 116/68 mm Hg. Which interpretation and next step by the nurse is most important?
options: Expected aging change; teach the client to rise quickly to limit dizziness
Orthostatic hypotension; ask which medications the client takes
No orthostatic change; recheck the BP after the client walks in the hall
Isolated systolic hypertension; ask how much salt the client eats daily
optionRationales: Incorrect. Orthostatic hypotension with a fall is not a normal aging change, and rising quickly worsens the drop; older adults should rise slowly and dangle first.

Correct. The systolic fell 26 mm Hg (≥20) with symptoms, which meets the criteria. Medications such as antihypertensives and diuretics are a leading cause in older adults, so asking about them is the most important next step.
Incorrect. A 26 mm Hg systolic drop meets orthostatic criteria, and walking a symptomatic client who has already fallen is unsafe.
Incorrect. The problem is a positional drop in BP, not a high systolic reading; sodium intake does not explain the lightheadedness on standing.
questions.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a systolic drop of 20 mm Hg or more or a diastolic drop of 10 mm Hg or more within 3 minutes of standing. Here the systolic fell 26 mm Hg and the client is symptomatic and has fallen. Older adults have slower compensatory reflexes and a decreased ability to adapt to cardiovascular stress. The slides also direct the nurse to find out whether an older adult takes antihypertensives, because medications increase the risk of orthostatic hypotension. Identifying the medication cause lets the nurse report it and plan fall prevention.
questions.takeaway: Older adult + ≥20 mm Hg systolic drop on standing + a fall → orthostatic hypotension; ask about BP and water pills.

questions.hintContent: Link the desirable values for each part of a lipid profile with the lifestyle goals taught for clients with hypertension (smoking, BMI, medications).
questions.hintStrategy: This is a negatively worded item: find the one client statement that is inaccurate. Check each lab-based statement against the individual lipid values, not just the total.
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with hypertension who smokes has a screening lipid profile: total cholesterol 186 mg/dL, LDL 168 mg/dL, HDL 34 mg/dL, triglycerides 142 mg/dL. After teaching, which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I will stop smoking completely instead of just cutting down.”
“I'll keep taking my BP pill even when my readings are normal.”
“My total cholesterol is under 200, so my lipids are fine.”
“I'm aiming for a body mass index below 25.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is accurate: there is no safe number of cigarettes, so quitting completely is the goal.
Incorrect. This is accurate: a normal reading shows the medication is working, and BP medications should not be skipped or stopped without the provider.

Correct — needs further teaching. A normal total can hide risk: the LDL of 168 is high (desirable under 100) and the HDL of 34 is low (desirable 40 or more in men, 50 or more in women), so both raise coronary artery disease risk.
Incorrect. This is accurate: the heart-healthy BMI goal is below 25.
questions.rationale: The lipid profile must be read part by part. This client's total cholesterol (186) and triglycerides (142) are desirable, but the LDL is high and the HDL is low, so the client still has a lipid-related coronary risk that needs provider follow-up and lifestyle change. The other statements match the teaching for a client with hypertension: quit smoking completely, keep BMI below 25, and never skip BP medication because a reading is normal.
questions.takeaway: A normal total cholesterol can hide a high LDL and low HDL — look at each part.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Stroke, Heart Failure, Pulmonary Edema & Hypertensive Crisis
questions.hintContent: Connect BE-FAST (sudden one-sided weakness and speech change), why swallowing may be unsafe after a stroke, and what each type of clot medication can and cannot do.
questions.hintStrategy: For each instruction, ask: does it get him to stroke care fast and keep him safe until he is evaluated, or does it delay care or add risk?
questions.stem: A telehealth nurse receives a call from a woman whose 70-year-old husband has atrial fibrillation. He suddenly cannot lift his right arm and his speech is garbled. Which instructions should the nurse give? Select all that apply.
options: Call 911 now instead of driving him to the hospital
Note the time he was last known to be normal
Give him sips of water so he can take his evening pills
Let him lie down and rest to see whether the weakness passes
Give him an extra dose of his anticoagulant to dissolve the clot
Do not give him anything to eat or drink until he is evaluated
optionRationales: Correct. Sudden one-sided arm weakness and speech changes are BE-FAST stroke signs; EMS starts care on the way and alerts the stroke team.
Correct. Time last known well guides treatment choices, including clot-dissolving medication, which depends on how much time has passed.
Incorrect. A stroke can impair swallowing, so even a sip can be aspirated; he stays NPO until a swallow screen is passed.
Incorrect. Waiting to see if symptoms pass wastes time — “time is brain.”
Incorrect. Anticoagulants prevent new clots and stop growth but do not dissolve an existing clot, and an extra dose adds bleeding risk before a CT has ruled out bleeding.
Correct. Keeping him NPO prevents aspiration until his swallow has been screened.
questions.rationale: Sudden right arm weakness and garbled speech are BE-FAST findings, and atrial fibrillation lets blood pool in the quivering atria and form clots that can travel to the brain. The caller should activate EMS and note the time last known well, because clot-dissolving therapy (a thrombolytic that activates plasmin) depends on time. Anticoagulants act on the coagulation cascade to prevent new clots; they do not dissolve an existing clot. Because a stroke can affect swallowing, nothing is given by mouth until a swallow screen is passed.
questions.takeaway: Stroke signs: call 911, note the last-known-well time, nothing by mouth — anticoagulants don't dissolve clots.

questions.hintContent: Combine the limbs that must not be used for BP, the reason for a palpated estimate in older adults with hypertension, and what the slides say to ask an older adult about BP.
questions.hintStrategy: For each action, decide whether it protects the client and gives a true reading, or whether it makes the reading falsely high or low.
questions.stem: The nurse observes a new graduate measure the blood pressure manually for a 78-year-old client who has long-standing hypertension and an arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm. Which actions by the new graduate are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Uses the right arm for the measurement
Palpates a systolic estimate before auscultating
Places the cuff over the client's thin sleeve
Asks whether the client takes antihypertensive medication
Reinflates the cuff right away on the same arm to confirm
Lets the client's arm hang down at the side of the chair
optionRationales: Correct. Cuff pressure on an arm with an AV fistula can clot it and ruin dialysis access.
Correct. Older adults with hypertension and stiff arteries often have an auscultatory gap; a palpated estimate prevents recording a falsely low systolic.
Incorrect. The cuff goes on bare skin; clothing makes the reading inaccurate (usually high).
Correct. The slides direct the nurse to determine whether an older adult takes antihypertensives, which affect the reading and the risk of hypotension.
Incorrect. Wait 1–2 minutes before repeating on the same arm so blood in the arm returns to normal.
Incorrect. An arm below heart level gives a falsely high reading; support the arm at heart level.
questions.rationale: Accurate BP in an older adult with hypertension combines site selection, technique, and age-specific assessment. The fistula arm is never used. Stiff, aging arteries make an auscultatory gap more likely, so the nurse palpates first and then inflates about 30 mm Hg above the estimate. The slides also tell the nurse to ask older adults about antihypertensives. Clothing under the cuff, immediate re-inflation, and a dangling arm all distort the reading.
questions.takeaway: Older adult with HTN: avoid the fistula arm, palpate first to catch a gap, ask about BP meds, bare arm at heart level.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Stroke, Heart Failure, Pulmonary Edema & Hypertensive Crisis
questions.hintContent: Trace where blood backs up when the left ventricle fails (which circulation sits behind it) and what a volume-overloaded ventricle sounds like.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding by where it comes from: the lungs and a volume-overloaded left ventricle, or the systemic veins behind the right heart.
questions.stem: A client is admitted with acute left-sided heart failure. Based on where blood backs up and how the weakened pump performs, which findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Crackles in both lung bases
A new S3 heard with the bell at the apex
Jugular vein distention with the head of the bed at 45°
Needing three pillows to breathe comfortably at night
2+ dependent pitting edema of both ankles
Abdominal fullness with a poor appetite
optionRationales: Correct. The left ventricle receives blood from the pulmonary circulation, so failure backs blood into the lungs and causes crackles.
Correct. An S3 in early diastole reflects blood rushing into a volume-overloaded ventricle and is a sign of heart failure in an adult.
Incorrect. JVD reflects back-up behind the right heart into the systemic veins — a right-sided finding.
Correct. Orthopnea results from pulmonary congestion that worsens when lying flat.
Incorrect. Dependent edema reflects systemic venous congestion from right-sided failure.
Incorrect. Abdominal fullness and poor appetite come from congestion of the body’s veins behind a failing right ventricle — a right-sided finding.
questions.rationale: Pulmonary and systemic circulations are in series. The left ventricle sits downstream of the lungs, so when it fails blood backs into the pulmonary circulation, causing crackles, dyspnea, and orthopnea (needing more pillows to breathe at night). The overloaded ventricle may also produce an S3 (“Ken-TUC-ky”). JVD, dependent edema, and abdominal fullness with poor appetite are backups behind the right ventricle into the body’s veins; they appear when right-sided failure develops, most often as a result of left-sided failure.
questions.takeaway: Left = Lungs (crackles, orthopnea, S3); Right = Rest of the body (JVD, edema, abdominal fullness).

questions.hintContent: Recall the basic life support steps for an adult who is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and pulseless.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option ask whether it gets high-quality compressions or defibrillation started faster, or whether it delays or dilutes them.
questions.stem: The nurse finds a client unresponsive in bed. The client is not breathing normally (only occasional gasps), and no carotid pulse is felt within 10 seconds. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Call for help and activate the emergency response system
Begin chest compressions at a rate of 100–120 per minute
Compress the chest at least 2 inches (5 cm) and allow full recoil
Recheck the pulse for a full 60 seconds before starting CPR
Give 2 rescue breaths after every 5 chest compressions
Attach the AED or defibrillator as soon as it arrives
optionRationales: Correct. Summoning help and the code team brings a defibrillator and additional rescuers.
Correct. Adult compressions are delivered at 100–120 per minute to maintain blood flow to the brain and heart.
Correct. Adequate depth with full chest recoil lets the heart refill between compressions.
Incorrect. A pulse check should take no more than 10 seconds; a longer check delays compressions.
Incorrect. The adult single-rescuer ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
Correct. Early defibrillation of a shockable rhythm is a key determinant of survival.
questions.rationale: CPR is one of the independent nursing interventions for perfusion: when the heart stops, perfusion stops. Occasional gasps are not normal breathing. For an unresponsive adult with no pulse, the nurse calls for help, starts high-quality compressions (100–120/min, at least 2 inches deep, full recoil), gives breaths at 30:2, and attaches the AED as soon as it is available.
questions.takeaway: No pulse, no normal breathing → call for help, push hard and fast (100–120/min, ≥2 in), 30:2, AED ASAP.

questions.hintContent: Connect venous stasis and clot formation with the independent actions that keep leg blood moving and the safe use of compression devices.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it keeps venous blood moving safely or whether it compresses the veins, creates a tourniquet, or could dislodge a clot.
questions.stem: A client is on postoperative day 1 after a hip replacement and has prescriptions for sequential compression devices (SCDs) and graduated compression stockings. Which actions by the nurse help prevent venous thrombosis safely? Select all that apply.
options: Measure the client's legs to select the correct device size
Check that two fingers fit between the SCD sleeve and the leg
Encourage ankle pumps every hour while the client is awake
Place a pillow under the client's knees for comfort
Roll the top of the stocking down if it is too long
Massage the client's calf if it becomes sore and warm
optionRationales: Correct. The wrong size either fails to compress or constricts the leg.
Correct. A two-finger fit confirms the sleeve is snug but not constrictive.
Correct. Calf-muscle action pushes venous blood back toward the heart and reduces venous stasis.
Incorrect. A pillow under the knees presses on the veins and promotes pooling.
Incorrect. A rolled stocking top forms a tight band that acts like a tourniquet.
Incorrect. A sore, warm calf may signal a clot; massage could dislodge it. Withhold compression on that leg and notify the provider.
questions.rationale: Pooled (static) blood in immobile legs is more likely to clot, and surgery plus bed rest raises the risk of venous thrombosis. The nurse keeps venous blood moving with independent measures (ankle pumps, early ambulation, fluids as allowed) and correctly applied compression devices (measured, two-finger fit, smooth, periodic skin checks). Knee pillows, rolled stockings, and massage either obstruct venous return or risk dislodging a clot.
questions.takeaway: Keep blood moving: correct size, two-finger fit, ankle pumps — no knee pillows, rolled stockings, or calf massage.

questions.hintContent: Connect the two big risks of catheterization (bleeding at the arterial puncture and contrast injury to the kidneys) with pulse-assessment technique and age-related kidney changes.
questions.hintStrategy: Keep actions that protect the femoral puncture, track distal blood flow consistently, or protect the kidneys; reject actions that flex the hip or mobilize too early.
questions.stem: A 78-year-old client returns to the unit after a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery. The right pedal pulse could be found only with a Doppler before the procedure. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Mark the Doppler pulse site on the skin so each check uses the same spot
Keep the right leg straight during prescribed bed rest
Keep the head of the bed at or below 30°
Encourage oral fluids and monitor urine output
Help the client sit up at 90° to eat lunch
Walk the client to the bathroom 30 minutes after arrival
optionRationales: Correct. Marking the Doppler site lets every nurse reassess the same location and detect a change in distal blood flow.
Correct. Hip flexion can disrupt the clot at the arterial puncture and cause bleeding.
Correct. Limiting head elevation keeps the groin from bending at the access site.
Correct. Fluids help flush the contrast; kidney filtration declines with age, so this client's kidneys are more vulnerable.
Incorrect. Sitting at 90° flexes the hip and increases the risk of bleeding and hematoma.
Incorrect. Early ambulation risks bleeding from the femoral puncture during prescribed bed rest.
questions.rationale: After femoral catheterization, the nurse protects the arterial puncture (leg straight, HOB 30° or less, bed rest as ordered) and checks distal pulses, color, temperature, and sensation. When a pulse is found only by Doppler, marking the spot ensures consistent reassessment. Contrast dye can injure the kidneys, and glomerular filtration falls 30–50% by age 80, so encouraging fluids and monitoring urine output are especially important in an older adult.
questions.takeaway: Femoral cath in an older adult: leg straight, HOB ≤30°, mark and recheck the Doppler pulse, fluids and urine output.

questions.hintContent: Combine the list of limbs where a BP cuff must not be used with the post-procedure care that protects an arterial access site.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each client separately: would inflating a cuff on the left arm damage a structure, interrupt therapy, or threaten a healing puncture?
questions.stem: The charge nurse is reviewing the vital-sign plan on a medical unit. For which clients should the nurse instruct the UAP not to use the left arm for blood pressure measurement? Select all that apply.
options: A client receiving hemodialysis through a left forearm arteriovenous fistula
A client who had a cardiac catheterization through the left radial artery today
A client who is left-handed and prefers the right arm to be free
A client who had a left mastectomy with axillary lymph node removal
A client with 0.9% sodium chloride infusing through a left forearm IV
A client with a large, healed tattoo on the left upper arm
optionRationales: Correct. Cuff pressure can clot the fistula and destroy the client's dialysis access.
Correct. After radial access, BP readings and blood draws are avoided on that arm to protect the puncture site and hand circulation.
Incorrect. Hand dominance does not affect BP measurement; either arm can be used.
Correct. Compression on the side of axillary node removal increases the risk of lymphedema.
Correct. Cuff inflation stops the infusion and can damage the vein.
Incorrect. A healed tattoo does not affect BP measurement.
questions.rationale: BP is not measured on a limb with an IV infusion, an AV fistula, axillary lymph node removal, a cast or bulky dressing, or injury or disease. The diagnostics lesson adds that after radial-artery catheterization, BP readings and blood draws are avoided on that arm while the arterial puncture heals. Hand dominance and tattoos do not matter. Use the other arm or the thigh.
questions.takeaway: No cuff on an arm with a fistula, infusing IV, node dissection, cast — or a fresh radial cath site.

questions.hintContent: Combine the difference between modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors with the desirable values on a lipid profile.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask two questions: is it actually a risk (compare labs with desirable values), and can the client change it?
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has these findings at a wellness visit: smokes 1 pack per day, LDL 162 mg/dL, HDL 52 mg/dL, BP 142/90 mm Hg, and a father who had an MI at age 48. Which findings should the nurse identify as modifiable cardiovascular risk factors to target? Select all that apply.
options: Cigarette smoking
Father's MI at age 48
LDL of 162 mg/dL
HDL of 52 mg/dL
Age of 55 years
BP of 142/90 mm Hg
optionRationales: Correct. Smoking is a modifiable risk factor; the goal is to quit completely.
Incorrect. Family history of early coronary artery disease is nonmodifiable.
Correct. LDL is above the desirable level of under 100 and can be lowered with diet, activity, weight loss, and prescribed medication.
Incorrect. An HDL of 52 exceeds the desirable level of 40 or more for men, so it is not a risk factor to target.
Incorrect. Age is nonmodifiable.
Correct. Elevated BP is a secondary risk factor that can be controlled with lifestyle changes and medication.
questions.rationale: Nonmodifiable risk factors include age, gender, race, and personal and family history. Modifiable and secondary factors include smoking, diet and BMI, activity, high BP, high cholesterol, stress, and alcohol. Reading the lipid profile part by part shows that this client's LDL is high, but his HDL is already desirable for a man, so it is not a target.
questions.takeaway: Target what is both abnormal and changeable: smoking, high LDL, high BP — not age, family history, or a healthy HDL.

questions.hintContent: Connect age-related vascular and pulmonary changes with how pulse pressure is calculated and which blood gas change always means disease.
questions.hintStrategy: Calculate any pulse pressure first, then sort each finding into expected aging change versus a finding that signals pathology — “common” is not always “normal.”
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing an 80-year-old client. Which findings are consistent with normal age-related cardiovascular and pulmonary changes? Select all that apply.
options: BP 148/76 mm Hg, a pulse pressure of 72 mm Hg
Slight decrease in arterial PaO₂
Increased anteroposterior chest diameter
PaCO₂ of 52 mm Hg on an arterial blood gas
New fatigue that now limits bathing and dressing
Pulse that takes longer to return to baseline after walking
optionRationales: Correct. Stiff, less elastic arteries raise the systolic pressure while the diastolic stays normal, widening the pulse pressure (148 − 76 = 72).
Correct. Arterial oxygen tension declines slightly with age.
Correct. Decreased chest wall compliance increases the anteroposterior diameter and residual volume.
Incorrect. An elevated PaCO₂ indicates pathology, not normal aging.
Incorrect. Fatigue and decreased activity are not normal aging and may be an atypical sign of a cardiac problem.
Correct. In older adults the pulse returns more slowly to baseline after exercise.
questions.rationale: With aging, arteries lose elasticity and develop lipid and calcium deposits, raising peripheral vascular resistance and often producing isolated systolic hypertension with a wide pulse pressure. Lung changes lower PaO₂ slightly and increase AP diameter, and the pulse recovers more slowly after exercise. An elevated PaCO₂ and new functional fatigue are never just aging — they need follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Aging: wide pulse pressure, slightly low PaO₂, barrel chest, slow pulse recovery; high PaCO₂ and new fatigue are not normal.

questions.hintContent: Connect the definition of a hypertensive emergency (target-organ damage) with how extreme afterload affects the left ventricle and which lab tests reveal heart and kidney injury.
questions.hintStrategy: The BP is the same either way. Keep only findings that show acute damage to the brain, heart, lungs, or kidneys.
questions.stem: A client with a history of nonadherence to antihypertensive medications has a BP of 214/126 mm Hg. Which additional findings indicate a hypertensive emergency rather than severe hypertension without organ damage? Select all that apply.
options: Severe headache with new confusion
Anxiety about being admitted to the hospital
Crackles throughout with pink, frothy sputum
Serum creatinine that rose from 1.0 to 2.4 mg/dL
Reports running out of medications 1 week ago
Troponin level that is rising on repeat draws
optionRationales: Correct. New confusion with severe headache shows acute brain (neurologic) damage.
Incorrect. Anxiety may raise BP but is not evidence of organ damage.
Correct. The left ventricle cannot eject against the extreme afterload, pressure backs into the lungs, and acute pulmonary edema results — lung damage.
Correct. A rising creatinine shows acute kidney damage.
Incorrect. Running out of medication explains the cause but is not organ damage.
Correct. Rising troponin on serial draws shows heart muscle injury.
questions.rationale: A hypertensive emergency is BP above about 180/120 plus acute target-organ damage. Very high BP means very high afterload, which raises the heart's oxygen demand and can back blood into the lungs (pulmonary edema) and injure the myocardium (rising troponin). The brain (new confusion) and kidneys (rising creatinine) are also targets. Anxiety and the reason for the high BP do not define an emergency.
questions.takeaway: It's the organ damage, not the number: confusion, pulmonary edema, rising troponin, rising creatinine.

questions.hintContent: Recall what the standing readings are compared against in orthostatic testing.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask which piece of data every later step depends on; that step must come first.
questions.stem: A client who reports dizziness has a prescription for orthostatic vital signs. The client is sitting in a bedside chair. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Assist the client to stand and measure the BP and pulse after 1 minute
Measure the BP and pulse while the client remains seated in the chair
Compare the client's current BP with the orthostatic criteria
Have the client lie supine for about 5 minutes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Standing readings are only meaningful when compared with a stable supine baseline, which must be obtained first.
Incorrect. A seated reading is not the baseline; orthostatic testing starts with the client lying supine after a rest period.
Incorrect. Criteria are applied only after supine and standing readings have both been obtained.
Correct. A stable supine baseline comes first: the client rests lying down for about 5 minutes before the first BP and pulse are measured.
questions.rationale: Orthostatic vital signs start with a stable supine baseline: the client lies supine for about 5 minutes, then BP and pulse are measured. The client is then assisted to stand (or sit if standing is unsafe) and readings are repeated at 1 and 3 minutes. A drop of 20 mm Hg or more systolic or 10 mm Hg or more diastolic is positive. The nurse stays with the client to prevent falls.
questions.takeaway: Orthostatic VS: supine rest ~5 min and baseline first, then stand and recheck at 1 and 3 minutes.

questions.hintContent: Connect the backup pacemaker rates (60–40–20), what a narrow QRS tells you about the ventricular pathway, and how heart rate affects cardiac output.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify which site is pacing from the rate and QRS width, then check whether the stated effect on filling or output matches that rate.
questions.stem: A client's SA node has stopped firing, and the monitor shows a regular rhythm at 48/min with a narrow QRS complex. BP is 92/58 mm Hg (baseline 124/76) and the client reports lightheadedness. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: The AV junction is pacing at its backup rate, so cardiac output falls
The Purkinje fibers are pacing at their backup rate, which narrows the QRS
The SA node is firing slowly, so a longer diastole lowers stroke volume
The AV junction is pacing, but its short diastole limits ventricular filling
optionRationales: Correct. The AV junction fires at 40–60/min and sends the impulse down the normal bundle of His–bundle branch–Purkinje path (narrow QRS). With CO = HR × SV, the slower rate lowers cardiac output, explaining the low BP and lightheadedness.
Incorrect. A ventricular (Purkinje) pacemaker fires at 20–40/min and produces a wide QRS, not a narrow one.
Incorrect. The SA node has stopped firing; a longer diastole allows more filling, not less stroke volume.
Incorrect. At 48/min diastole is longer, not shorter; the problem is too few beats, not too little filling.
questions.rationale: When the SA node fails, the AV junction takes over at 40–60/min. The impulse still travels through the bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers, so the QRS stays narrow and the ventricles contract. Because cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume, a rate of 48 can drop cardiac output enough to lower BP and cause lightheadedness — a new rhythm with symptoms that the nurse reports.
questions.takeaway: Junctional rhythm (40–60, narrow QRS): normal ventricular pathway, but the slow rate can drop cardiac output.

questions.hintContent: Connect the apical-radial technique with why an irregular rhythm produces beats that never reach the wrist (think about filling time and stroke volume).
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option: does it keep the two counts simultaneous and complete, and does any interpretation match the physiology of a pulse deficit?
questions.stem: Two nurses are obtaining an apical-radial pulse on a client with atrial fibrillation. Which actions or interpretations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Count each rate for 30 seconds and multiply by 2
Locate the apical pulse at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line
Use one watch and a single signal, counting both rates together for 60 seconds
Count the radial rate first, then the apical rate when the radial count is done
Record a radial rate of 104 and an apical rate of 96 as a pulse deficit of 8
Recognize that a deficit reflects beats too weak to reach the wrist because the ventricles had little time to fill
optionRationales: Incorrect. An irregular rhythm must be counted for a full 60 seconds; shorter counts multiply the error.
Correct. The apical pulse is heard at the apex, the 5th intercostal space at the left midclavicular line.
Correct. One timepiece, a shared start, and a full minute ensure both nurses count the same beats.
Incorrect. Counting at different times does not compare the same beats, so a true deficit cannot be measured.
Incorrect. The radial rate can never exceed the apical rate; this indicates a counting error and must be recounted.
Correct. In an irregular rhythm, early beats come before the ventricles fill, so stroke volume is too small to create a palpable radial pulse.
questions.rationale: The pulse is the wave of blood from left ventricular contraction and reflects stroke volume. In atrial fibrillation, some beats come so early that diastolic filling is too short; those beats are heard at the apex but not felt at the wrist. Two nurses count apical and radial rates simultaneously for a full minute with one watch, and the difference (apical − radial) is the pulse deficit. A radial rate higher than the apical rate is always an error.
questions.takeaway: Pulse deficit = apical − radial, counted together for 60 s; missing radial beats are poorly filled beats.

questions.hintContent: Connect why the motor pathways cross, the typical behavior after a right-hemisphere stroke, where clots come from in atrial fibrillation, and what a thrombolytic actually does.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement against two things: the side and behavior pattern of a right-hemisphere stroke, and the correct mechanism of clot formation and clot-dissolving therapy.
questions.stem: A client with atrial fibrillation has an ischemic stroke of the right cerebral hemisphere. The nurse is precepting a nursing student. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: “Expect weakness of his left arm and leg.”
“Expect him to have trouble understanding and forming words.”
“The clot likely formed in his quivering atria and traveled to the brain.”
“Place his call light on his left side to help him notice that side.”
“His impulsivity makes fall prevention a top priority.”
“Alteplase works by preventing new clots, not by breaking this one down.”
optionRationales: Correct. Motor tracts cross, so a right-hemisphere stroke causes left-sided weakness.
Incorrect. Aphasia is typical of a left-hemisphere stroke; with a right-hemisphere stroke, speech may be slurred but language is usually intact.
Correct. In atrial fibrillation, blood pools in the quivering atria and forms clots that can travel to the brain.
Incorrect. With left neglect he will not notice items on the left; the call light belongs on his right (noticed) side.
Correct. Right-hemisphere strokes cause impulsivity and overestimation of abilities, so falls are a major risk.
Incorrect. Alteplase is manufactured tPA; it activates plasmin, which digests fibrin and dissolves the existing clot.
questions.rationale: Atrial fibrillation lets blood pool and clot in the atria; an embolus can lodge in a brain artery and cause an ischemic stroke. Because motor pathways cross, a right-hemisphere stroke causes left-sided weakness, left neglect, and impulsivity, so the nurse keeps the call light on the right and prioritizes fall prevention. Aphasia points to the left hemisphere. Thrombolytics such as alteplase act on fibrinolysis — they activate plasmin to dissolve the clot — unlike anticoagulants, which only prevent new clots.
questions.takeaway: A-fib clot → right-brain stroke → left weakness, left neglect, impulsive; alteplase dissolves the clot via plasmin.

questions.hintContent: Connect B.E.'s heart failure history with what too much preload does to a weak ventricle and why his urine output is low.
questions.hintStrategy: Keep interventions that monitor fluid balance, reduce venous return, or protect the airway; reject any that add volume, raise preload, or add aspiration risk.
questions.stem: B.E., 64, with a history of heart failure, is 36 hours post ischemic stroke. He has bilateral crackles, pitting edema of the legs, urine output of 15 mL/hr, and difficulty managing secretions. Which interventions are indicated at this time? Select all that apply.
options: Administer a 1,000 mL normal saline bolus for the low urine output
Obtain daily weights on the same scale at the same time
Offer thin oral liquids to prevent dehydration
Maintain strict intake and output
Elevate the head of the bed at least 30°
Lay him flat with his legs raised to improve kidney blood flow
optionRationales: Incorrect. The low urine output reflects low cardiac output with fluid overload; a bolus adds preload to an overstretched ventricle and worsens pulmonary congestion.
Correct. Daily weights under consistent conditions are the best measure of fluid gain or loss.
Incorrect. He cannot manage secretions, so thin liquids risk aspiration; he is NPO and is not dehydrated.
Correct. Strict I&O tracks fluid balance and the response to treatment such as diuretics.
Correct. Head elevation eases breathing, reduces venous return to the heart, and lowers aspiration risk.
Incorrect. Lying flat with legs raised increases venous return (preload) and fluid in the lungs and raises aspiration risk.
questions.rationale: B.E.'s crackles, edema, and falling urine output mean fluid overload with a pump that can't keep up — his kidneys are underperfused, not dry. Continuously overstretched muscle fibers (high preload) contract less effectively, so anything that adds volume or venous return (a bolus, lying flat with legs up) makes things worse. Care focuses on fluid monitoring (daily weights, strict I&O), head elevation, airway protection, and prescribed diuretics.
questions.takeaway: Low urine + crackles + edema in HF = overload, not dehydration: weigh, strict I&O, HOB up — no bolus, no legs up.

questions.hintContent: Connect the normal cardiovascular and blood changes of pregnancy with the extra heart sound that can be normal late in pregnancy and the clotting changes that raise venous thrombosis risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Mark each finding as an expected adaptation of the third trimester or an abnormal change, then select only the abnormal ones.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for a client at 32 weeks' gestation. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Resting pulse 12 bpm higher than her prepregnancy baseline
An S3 heard at the apex with clear lungs and normal SpO₂
Hematocrit of 34%
BP of 150/98 mm Hg on two readings
WBC count of 13,000/mm³ with no signs of infection
Swelling, warmth, and pain in the right calf only
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cardiac output increases and the pulse normally rises about 10–15 bpm by term.
Incorrect. With high blood volume and a compliant ventricle, an S3 is expected in the third trimester when the client has no other findings.
Incorrect. Plasma expands more than red cells, so a slightly lower hematocrit is expected.
Correct. BP normally falls in pregnancy; a BP above prepregnancy levels needs prompt evaluation.
Incorrect. Leukocyte production normally increases in pregnancy and does not indicate infection.
Correct. Fibrinogen and clotting factors VII, VIII, IX, and X rise and the uterus slows venous return, so one-sided calf swelling, warmth, and pain suggests venous thrombosis.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy raises cardiac output, pulse (10–15 bpm), blood volume (40–50%), leukocytes, and clotting factors, and slightly lowers hematocrit. The expanded volume can produce a normal S3 in the third trimester. Rising BP and signs of a leg clot are not normal: clotting time stays about the same, but increased clotting factors plus venous stasis from the enlarging uterus raise venous thrombosis risk.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy: faster pulse, S3, lower Hct, higher WBC are expected; high BP and a swollen, painful calf are not.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Connect the main risk after arterial catheterization with how blood loss changes pulse pressure and heart rate, and what an expected post-procedure site looks like.
questions.hintStrategy: Calculate the pulse pressure in any BP given and compare it with the earlier value; separate stable expected findings from one showing compensation for volume loss.
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client 3 hours after a cardiac catheterization via the left femoral artery. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
options: Pedal pulses 2+ and equal in both feet, with warm toes
BP 106/90 and HR 116, from 132/78 and 82 on arrival
Small bruise at the site that is not enlarging
Urine output of 60 mL/hr since the procedure
optionRationales: Incorrect. Equal 2+ pulses and warm toes show that blood flow to the leg is preserved.

Correct. The pulse pressure has narrowed from 54 to 16 mm Hg and the heart rate has risen — compensation for blood loss, which can be internal even when the site looks dry. Assess the site and notify the provider now.
Incorrect. Minor, stable bruising at an arterial puncture site is expected.
Incorrect. Adequate urine output suggests the kidneys are tolerating the contrast.
questions.rationale: Bleeding is a major risk after arterial catheterization. As volume falls, less blood returns to the heart (lower preload), stroke volume and systolic pressure fall, and the body constricts vessels and speeds the heart, keeping the diastolic up. The result is a narrowing pulse pressure with a rising heart rate — an early sign of poor perfusion even before the systolic looks dangerously low. Equal pulses, a stable bruise, and good urine output are expected.
questions.takeaway: After cath: narrowing pulse pressure + rising HR = bleeding until proven otherwise.

questions.hintContent: Connect how pulse pressure is calculated with the age-related changes in the arterial wall and the determinants of blood pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Do the calculation first, then check each statement about the cause against what aging does to the vessels.
questions.stem: An 82-year-old client has a blood pressure of 168/72 mm Hg. Which statements about this client's blood pressure are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The pulse pressure is 72 mm Hg
The pulse pressure is 96 mm Hg
The reading is consistent with orthostatic hypotension
The reading is consistent with isolated systolic hypertension
Loss of arterial elasticity with aging increases peripheral vascular resistance
A decrease in blood viscosity with aging raises the systolic pressure
optionRationales: Incorrect. 72 mm Hg is the diastolic pressure, not the difference between systolic and diastolic.
Correct. Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 168 − 72 = 96 mm Hg.
Incorrect. Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in BP on standing, which a single reading cannot show.
Correct. A high systolic pressure with a normal diastolic pressure is isolated systolic hypertension, common in older adults.
Correct. Stiff, less compliant arteries increase peripheral vascular resistance and raise systolic pressure.
Incorrect. Decreased viscosity would lower, not raise, resistance and BP; it is not the age-related cause.
questions.rationale: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic: 168 − 72 = 96 mm Hg, which is wide. With aging, arteries lose elasticity, the intimal and medial layers thicken, and lipid and calcium deposits form. Loss of arterial compliance increases peripheral vascular resistance, so each beat hits a stiff pipe: systolic spikes, but the stiff walls recoil poorly, so diastolic stays normal — isolated systolic hypertension.
questions.takeaway: Pulse pressure = SBP − DBP; stiff aging arteries → wide pulse pressure and isolated systolic hypertension.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Cardiac Output, Preload, Afterload & Contractility
questions.hintContent: Connect what a very fast rate does to diastolic filling, stroke volume, and cardiac output with when the coronary arteries fill.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether the findings show compensation or failing output, then choose the action that addresses a failing pump and starving myocardium rather than one that delays care or needs a prescription.
questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease had a heart rate of 80/min and a stroke volume of 70 mL (cardiac output 5.6 L/min). The heart rate suddenly rises to 170/min, BP falls from 124/76 to 86/52 mm Hg, and the client reports chest tightness and lightheadedness. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage slow, deep breaths and recheck vital signs in 30 minutes
Infuse a 500 mL normal saline bolus to restore ventricular filling
Help the client walk in the hall to ease anxiety and slow the rate
Obtain an ECG as ordered and notify the provider now
optionRationales: Incorrect. A very fast rate with falling BP and chest tightness is failing cardiac output; waiting 30 minutes delays care.
Incorrect. The problem is too little filling time, not too little volume, and a bolus requires a prescription.
Incorrect. Activity raises myocardial oxygen demand and is unsafe with chest tightness and hypotension.
Correct. A very fast rate with falling BP and chest pain means cardiac output is failing and the myocardium is not getting enough oxygen; obtain an ECG as ordered and notify the provider now.
questions.rationale: CO = HR × SV. At 170/min diastole is so short that the ventricles cannot fill, so stroke volume, cardiac output, and BP fall despite the faster rate. Diastole is also when the coronary arteries fill; with narrowed coronaries and a short diastole, the heart muscle is starved of oxygen, causing chest tightness. Very fast heart rate with falling BP and lightheadedness is a red flag: stop activity, obtain an ECG as ordered, and notify the provider now.
questions.takeaway: Very fast HR → short diastole → less ventricular and coronary filling → falling CO and chest pain: ECG and notify now.

questions.hintContent: Recall what distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from severe hypertension alone.
questions.hintStrategy: Use ABCs: find the finding that shows acute organ damage threatening breathing.
questions.stem: B.E., 64, is on day 4 after an ischemic stroke and is mechanically ventilated. BP is 258/128 mm Hg and P 112. During a sedation vacation he is minimally responsive and grimaces as if in pain. The nurse suspects a hypertensive emergency. Which finding requires the nurse's most immediate follow-up?
options: Heart rate of 112/min with an irregular rhythm on the monitor
Minimal responsiveness during the sedation vacation
Pink, frothy secretions and crackles throughout the lungs
Grimacing and brow furrowing when he is repositioned
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tachycardia is nonspecific and is not evidence of acute organ damage.
Incorrect. Decreased responsiveness is nonspecific in a sedated, ventilated client and is not the most urgent threat here.
Correct. Pink frothy secretions with diffuse crackles indicate acute pulmonary edema — target-organ damage that defines a hypertensive emergency and threatens oxygenation.
Incorrect. Pain raises sympathetic tone and BP and should be treated, but it is a contributing factor, not the life-threatening organ damage.
questions.rationale: BP above 180/120 with acute target-organ damage — here, acute pulmonary edema (pink frothy secretions and crackles throughout) — defines a hypertensive emergency and is a breathing threat. Tachycardia and decreased responsiveness are nonspecific. His grimacing suggests pain, which raises sympathetic tone and BP, so pain should also be assessed and treated along with the controlled BP lowering prescribed by the provider.
questions.takeaway: Hypertensive emergency = BP >180/120 + acute organ damage (e.g., pulmonary edema); treat pain as a contributor.

questions.ref: Module 16 · Perfusion · Health Promotion, Independent & Collaborative Interventions
questions.hintContent: Connect what cardiac rehabilitation and nonpharmacologic therapies include, how the nurse handles supplements, and why keeping leg blood moving prevents clots after surgery.
questions.hintStrategy: Keep statements that are accurate and promote safe collaboration or circulation; reject ones that give false reassurance, promote stasis, or harm BP control.
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client is being discharged after heart surgery and mentions plans to start herbal supplements and chelation therapy that a friend recommended. Which statements by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: “Rest in bed as much as possible until your incision has fully healed.”
“Cardiac rehabilitation will give you supervised exercise, education, and counseling.”
“Natural products are safe because they do not interact with heart medications.”
“Please review any supplements or chelation therapy with your provider before starting.”
“Add a little extra salt to your meals so your blood pressure does not drop.”
“Short walks and ankle pumps keep blood from pooling and clotting in your legs.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Prolonged bed rest causes venous stasis and deconditioning; cardiac rehabilitation promotes progressive, supervised activity.
Correct. Cardiac rehabilitation provides supervised, progressive exercise with education and counseling.
Incorrect. Some supplements affect bleeding, BP, or heart rhythm and can interact with prescribed medications.
Correct. The nurse neither dismisses nor endorses these therapies but asks the client to review every product with the provider.
Incorrect. A heart-healthy diet limits sodium; salt causes fluid retention and raises BP.
Correct. Calf-muscle activity pushes venous blood back to the heart; pooled blood is more likely to clot.
questions.rationale: Collaborative therapies include surgery, cardiac rehabilitation, medications, and nonpharmacologic measures such as diet, exercise, and supplements, which the client should review with the provider because some interact with medications or affect bleeding. After surgery, venous stasis raises the risk of venous thrombosis, so walking and ankle pumps — not prolonged bed rest — keep leg blood moving. Extra salt works against BP and fluid control.
questions.takeaway: After heart surgery: cardiac rehab, review all supplements with the provider, keep moving to prevent clots.
